Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Secretary of State for External Affairs, of which I have given notice. I should like to ask, in view of the statement by the Secretary General of the

United Nations yesterday that he has proposed the cessation of bombing of North Viet Nam, the scaling down of military activities in South Viet Nam, and a willingness to deal with the Viet Cong as three initial steps toward peace in that unhappy country, if the minister would inform the house whether the Canadian government is prepared to make these steps the basis of its policies, and to urge the government of the United States to accept them as well.

maintopic: REPORTED SPEECH BY INDUSTRY MINISTER RESPECTING NEWS COVERAGE

subsubtopic: VIET NAM-STEPS PROPOSED BY UN SECRETARY GENERAL

Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend was kind enough to give me notice of his intention to ask this question. The government shares the concern of the Secretary General with respect to the continuing hostilities in Viet Nam, not only because of the human suffering involved but because of the effects for world peace inherent in this conflict. We have been in touch with the Secretary General on these problems and have discussed these matters with him.
The diplomatic initiatives in which Canada is engaged are designed to determine whether a mutually acceptable basis for a negotiated settlement exists. I believe my hon. friend would agree that Mr. Ronning having just returned to Canada, and our having just begun our discussions with him, and being now engaged here and elsewhere in discussions with other governments concerned, it would not help what we are seeking to do to take particular positions in this way when they would be bound to prejudice what we have in mind.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF PROGRAM TO ASSIST PERSONS IN NEED

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Tuesday, June 14, consideration in committee of the following
Canada Assistance Plan resolution-Mr. MacEachen-Mr. Batten in the chair:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure, to be known as the Canada Assistance Plan, to establish a program for sharing with the provinces in the cost of assistance, including health care and welfare services, provided to or in respect of persons in need, including mothers and children, older persons, disabled persons and unemployed persons who are in need, and in the cost of developing and improving assistance and welfare services programs including child and youth welfare programs throughout Canada; to provide for the making of arrangements for extending provincial welfare programs, with the approval of Indian bands, to Indians with reserve status, and for the making of payments to the provinces with respect to the cost of so extending those programs; to provide for the making of payments to the provinces with respect to the cost of specialized projects for assisting and rehabilitating persons in need or likely to become persons in need who have unusual difficulty in obtaining or holding employment; to provide for amendments to the Old Age Assistance Act, the Blind Persons Act, the Disabled Persons Act and the Unemployment Assistance Act that are incidental to or consequential on the introduction of the Canada Assistance Plan; and to provide further for the extension of the Established Programs (Interim Arrangements) Act to the Canada Assistance Plan.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this resolution was discussed one week ago, and I am pleased that it did not carry at that time. I have a few words to say on this matter. I might start out by saying we do support the resolution. I think it should be completely understood, however, that this is not any end-all to welfare legislation; it is purely a tidying up operation and there really is nothing new in it. It appears to me that in this 1966-67 fiscal year we simply are taking over $85 million of expenditure which previously was undertaken by the provinces. This is going to be paid by the federal government and, as I see it, we are going to co-ordinate and tidy up these pieces of legislation.
I am for that; let this not be mistaken. During my term of office I contemplated some operation of this kind. I recall so well when, during my term of office, we proposed any of our many advanced and improved pieces of welfare legislation the then hon. member for Essex East, at present the Secretary of State for External Affairs, made many blatant claims to having instituted all the good legislation ever put on the statute books of Canada. I remember one evening he was putting on such a good show that I became very impressed and offered him a position as an actor with the Stratford Shakespearean festival; his acting was really that good. If I

June 21, 1966
Canada Assistance Plan might digress for a moment, while I know his birthday is not until Thursday I should like to wish the Secretary of State for External Affairs the best of everything for that day.
Again, Mr. Chairman, I repeat that this is only a showpiece of legislation. I should like to examine some of the minister's remarks when he opened the discussion on this resolution. I know this government would like to have the people of Canada forget just what has been done in the past by way of welfare legislation, and I should like to outline some of the accomplishments in this field under the government of the right hon. Leader of the Opposition.
The last original set of estimates for the Department of National Health and Welfare prepared by our government in 1963 for the fiscal year 1963-64 provided $1,205 million. The last set of estimates by the previous St. Laurent government, for the fiscal year 1957-58, totalled $525,500,000. This is an increase of $679,500,000 in a period of six years. The increase in that period is approximately 130 per cent. I would point out that both these figures exclude any reference to old age security. We know what happened there. Immediately the house sat after our government took over in 1957 the old age security payment was raised from $46 to $55 a month, effective November 1, 1957. Effective February 1, 1962 the old age security payment was raised from $55 to $65 a month. These increases also immediately went to the recipients of old age assistance, recipients of the blind persons allowance and recipients of the disabled persons allowance; they were effective on the same date.
Then we remember that great period early in 1963. Big things were supposed to come about. We had the presumed 60 days of decision coming before us. Those days of decision were supposed to include presentation of a Canada pension plan. We remember what happened to that; it fell apart. Some three or four efforts later we did have a pension plan. The original plan suggested an immediate increase to $75 a month in the old age security payment, but this had to be withdrawn, as we well know. It was only through pressure by the official opposition when the house reconvened, I believe on September 30 of that year, that an increase in the old age security payment to $75 a month then became effective. The government neglected the recipients of the old age security, the blind persons allowances and the disabled

persons allowances; their increase did not come about until 1964.
This government has allowed an increase in the cost of living which is incomprehensible to the people in these categories, the people who receive these allowances and who cannot get along without them. We know that old age security should be $100 a month today. Earlier this session we brought in an amendment to the effect that the recipients of old age security and these other allowances should receive $100 a month. Our motion was defeated by the people in the far left corner of the house; we would have had it except for that party.
A week ago today the hon. member for Simcoe East dealt with the need for this increase. We claim it is needed now, not sometime in the future. Only this morning I was speaking to a social worker who indicated the gross need for some help, some alleviation of the conditions under which these people are living. She mentioned one person who is existing almost entirely on shredded wheat. Another family had had no meat for quite a long period. These things are before us, Mr. Chairman-these needs, these requirements. This is the reason I claim we should act now to increase the old age security to $100 a month.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
In his remarks a week ago the minister mentioned unemployment assistance. I should like to point out just what did transpire in respect of unemployment assistance. When we came into office in 1957 there was a 4.5 per cent minimum below which the federal government would not participate with the provinces in unemployment assistance. What happened? In the estimate for this item in the Department of National Health and Welfare for the year 1963-64, to which I referred earlier, the last prepared by our government, the amount was $110 million. For the year 1957-58, the last year in which the St. Laurent government prepared estimates, the figure for unemployment assistance was $5,125,000. This is an increase of approximately $105 million, from $5 million to $110 million. This indicates the welfare assistance steps that were taken by our government in an effort to assist the needy.
The minister spoke of supplementary payments to recipients of welfare assistance, and a huge part of the increase I mentioned from $5 million to $110 million is represented by these payments to various categories of welfare recipients. The government during the
June 21, 1966

last election campaign seemed to indicate that this increase represented something new and that something over the $75 per month to the aged would be paid. The government tried to hoodwink the people by suggesting that old age assistance would amount to something in the neighbourhood of $125 per month. I can show you legislation on the statute books which indicates that any amount of money which is paid by way of a supplemental allowance is shared between the federal and provincial governments on a 50-50 basis.
This house and the country are aware of the advance in social legislation initiated by the government of which I had the honour to be a member. I claim without any risk of contradiction that the greatest strides in social welfare to be taken in the history of Canada were taken when the Progressive Conservative party was in power.
I should like to refer to a few things about which the minister spoke in presenting this resolution. He referred to mothers' allowances and I am pleased that this type of assistance is to be given. When I was the minister a suggestion was made to the various provinces that if they changed their legislation our legislation could be interpreted in such a way that assistance in the form of mothers' allowances could be brought under the category of unemployment assistance. This suggestion was followed and involved a large portion of the increase in assistance from $5 million to $110 million over a six-year period. In any event, I am pleased that as a result of this resolution mothers' allowances will be supported by the federal government.
The minister also referred to health care costs which are to be brought within the proposed legislation. While it is true that people are receiving health care assistance from the provinces at this time, under this proposal the federal government will share in the cost.
Let me repeat that what is really happening is a transfer of payments. Instead of the provinces paying these costs alone the federal government is now going to assist. I am not against such a proposal but let us not forget that this legislation will not provide something new.
The minister said that the government intends to continue to contribute to existing categorical programs for the aged, blind and disabled. I assume this will involve a phasing out operation and that eventually these programs will disappear. He also suggested an
Canada Assistance Plan extension of provincial welfare programs to Indians who are now living on reserves, crown land or unorganized territory. It is my belief that this type of assistance was provided formerly by the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources through the Indian affairs branch. I realize that certain medical services were provided for Indians on reservations by the Department of National Health and Welfare and I am pleased to note that this whole program will be brought under the one department.
I was impressed by the minister's remarks which indicated that he was pressing for assistance to the severely retarded who have a limited employment potential. This potential can be developed if they are given an opportunity to partake in meaningful activity. This is a very worth-while step. We all know of the existence of private organizations which participate in this type of endeavour, and the one which occurs to me immediately is Marina Creations. I happen to be fairly well acquainted with this organization and I recall a visit made to my office by Mrs. George A. Marshall of Toronto at which time she set forth the work they were doing on behalf of the handicapped. This is worthwhile work and government funds should be made available in this regard.
Under this kind of a program the handicapped are taught to use the abilities they have. Some of them are not able to do much but through programs of this kind they are taught self-respect. Some of them even reach self-sufficiency to the point that they pay income tax.
During the last election campaign the Progressive Conservative party proposed that the means test be discarded in respect of retarded and disabled people. Certainly these people deserve assistance and encouragement in living their own lives and I am pleased that the minister has made some mention of assistance in this direction.
The minister spoke in glowing terms of the proposed legislation and suggested that it will cost an additional $85 million during the 1966-67 fiscal year. In this regard I should like to emphasize the words quoted by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre when he referred to a speech made by the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare in Fredericton on June 2 of this year. She said on that occasion that she wanted to make two general points. The first was that this plan does not involve any grand new programs. She said
June 21, 1966

Canada Assistance Plan the second point was that although the plan would operate under the umbrella of a federal statute and receive substantial financial support from the federal government the details of the various programs and administrative responsibility would rest with the provinces.
I conclude by saying that what this plan amounts to is really a tidying up operation which is completely inadequate for the needs of people in these welfare categories. Let us not be fooled by the government when it refers to supplementary benefits because any thought that there are additional benefits to be received is wrong and only a delusion. We should provide $100 a month now for our older citizens.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in considering the legislation under discussion one must congratulate the federal government for recognizing its responsibility to assume a greater share of the cost of providing supplementary assistance to the needy. I hope the government continues to recognize this necessity and thereby relieves provincial governments of a portion of the growing burden of welfare costs. It is doing so to the extent that a tax rearrangement is taking place and there is greater recognition of the federal role to be played in Canada. These changes are gratifying.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
What disturbs me about this legislation is the implication that this is in effect what the government is offering the senior citizens of Canada in response to their urgent needs. If this is so, if the government is using this legislation as a red herring to relieve itself of its responsibilities to our senior citizens, then this government must stand condemned in the strongest possible terms. This is part of the phony war on poverty, and I use these words advisedly because of a deep feeling of anger at having to stand by on this side of the house and watch the government lightly ignore the pressing needs of our senior citizens. At times the purpose of this legislation appears to be little more than to convince those who are prosperous in this country that the needs of those who are poor are being met. Yet this is not so. The needs of our senior citizens and of our disadvantaged are simply not being met by the legislation that the government is introducing at the present time.
It is difficult to understand how the government can ignore the almost universal
[Mr. Monteith.l

pleas on behalf of the older people in this; country after listening to hon. members in all sections of the house, including the government side, who have spoken and called for an increase in the old age pension. The only-reason I can find for such lack of action is that the government thinks it is fairly safe in office. Although it is a minority government, it is fairly obvious that very few people in Canada want an election and because the government has assessed the mood of the country it thinks it can maintain itself in office.
Let me speak for myself in this respect. I do not wish to see another election any more-than anyone else, especially when we consider the number of elections that have taken place recently. However, if we are going to-have to defeat the government in order to get increased old age pensions for our senior citizens, than I think this government should be defeated and the sooner the better because positive action must be taken. This government is playing at politics although they know they have to do something for the older people in Canada. What are they waiting for? Will they hold off action on this matter until just before an election so they can look like geniuses and heroes at that time? Will they ignore the present needs and stand by and watch the kind of suffering that is taking place among our senior citizens before they do anything? I would certainly hope that will not be the case but we have had no indication that the government's intention is to do anything other than that.
The government has been saying that it cannot afford to increase old age pensions and in the very same breath it speaks of the fantastic progress that has been made in this country. They brag about our great $51 billion economy and they talk about the most affluent of times under the jurisdiction of the Liberal party. Affluent for whom and affluent for what? What sense of values have they when they say "this great affluent society, this great $51 billion economy", and in the same breath say "there is no money for our older people?" In my opinion Canada can very well afford to treat its senior citizens with decency.
It is interesting to note that Canada in comparison with other western nations has far fewer people over the age of 60. In the booklet called "The Aging Worker In The Canadian Economy" dated July, 1964 it is stated that only 10.8 per cent of our population are 60 years and over. Of course the
June 21, 1966

percentage of those who are 65 and over is *even smaller. We can draw the conclusion from this information that an affluent society can easily afford to give increased support and sustenance to the small proportion of its people who require assistance. In Canada 10.8 per cent of our population are over 60; in Australia, 12.2 per cent; New Zealand, 12.2 per cent; the Netherlands, 13.3 per cent; the United States, 13.2 per cent and Sweden 17.3 per cent. In view of the resources of our *country and our working population there is no reason to assume that we cannot provide this increased assistance to our older citizens.
We hear about priorities. The government says that education and other matters have a greater priority than old age assistance. No one denies the importance of these other matters and no one denies the need for education, medicare, etc., but what can have greater priority than the giving of assistance to those who require it? If necessary, some of these other matters can wait but this matter cannot wait because the hand of time will not wait for our senior citizens. Every month and every year that go by mean that a portion of their lives which could have been a little more worth while and a little more livable has been lost to them.
This situation requires some elementary justice. We have heard eloquent speeches from both sides of the house on why this country should carry out its obligation toward its senior citizens. These are the people who built this country. These are the people who lived in less than affluent times and who did not have the opportunity to put aside sufficient money for their old age despite the fact that they probably worked much harder than does the present generation.
Let me refer again to the information contained in "The Aging Worker In The Canadian Economy" regarding the educational level of our senior citizens aged 65 and over. It is said there that 65.6 per cent of them reached no higher than the elementary school level. The reason for this was certainly not their lack of interest in furthering their education but simply that it was not possible for them to do so. It is these people who have made it possible for those of us who are younger, for those now in school or who have been in school recently, to acquire a higher and fuller education.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
Does this generation not owe at least something to them? Does it not have a duty to see that they get some minimum standard of
Canada Assistance Plan living? When we talk about an old age pension of $100 a month we are not talking about the moon. We are not talking about a sum of money to enable our older citizens to live in affluence. At this time $100 per month will do little more than retrieve the erosion that has taken place in the $75. The old age pensioners are not only not advancing, not only not keeping up with the increased rewards of productivity and increased benefits obtainable in our society, but keep slipping inexorably behind. I do not know what the $75 would be worth in actual value today but it certainly would not buy as much as it would have three years ago. An increase in the pension at this time would do little more than put pensioners in the same position they were a few years ago.
Is this such a great thing to demand in an affluent society? Is this such a great thing to ask of the country? Is this too great a burden to place upon the working population, to ask our young people to provide some assistance for the generation that not only fought our wars in many cases but through their sacrifices built up public services and an educational system for the benefit of those who followed? I do not believe it is too great a sacrifice. I think it is a sacrifice our people would willingly make if the government would provide them with that opportunity. How can we stand by in Canada and see our resources used inadequately, and yet talk about not being able to afford things?
It seems to me that if this government had some better philosophy, some better attitude toward the management of this country, they would find that an efficient use of our natural resources would be adequate to the task of assisting our senior citizens. We heard a big hint earlier today when the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre questioned the minister about the plans he had and whether he had any other ideas for helping the senior citizens of Canada. The member for Winnipeg North Centre did not receive much information.
There is a report from the Senate that calls for a different kind of program than a flat rate, old age pension. It is a good report and contains some worth-while ideas. In the years ahead the old age pension may not be the only answer to the problems of our senior citizens. What is the alternative? Has the government any other answer? Is the government considering any other program? Has it any hope to

Canada Assistance Plan offer the people of Canada who need assistance now or is the government merely obscuring the issue in such a way as to deny responsibility? Is this a way of procrastinating, a way for the government to drag its feet? Certainly it is not helping.
Occasionally we hear, and we have heard this from the government, that any increase in the pension would be inflationary. When the economy is bad the government says, we cannot afford these things. When the economy is good, increases in old age pensions become inflationary. No matter what happens in this country, whether we have high unemployment or low unemployment, whether we have prosperity or a depression, when it comes to increases in old age pensions the government says either that we cannot afford it or it is going to be inflationary. So far no one on the government side has said that the older people of this country do not deserve it. They would not dare to say this.
However, the government does assert entirely contradictory points of view. They say we cannot afford it and that it is inflationary. The government often asks, where are you going to get the money? When the government says that increases in old age pensions will be inflationary, I do not think they know what they are talking about. We look around and see the kind of spending that is going on in those sectors of the economy that are truly under some pressure and it does not make sense to see expenditures that really are inflationary. What is happening is that the government is not prepared to stop inflation in those sectors in which it should be stopped.
What is the older person going to do with an increase in the old age pension? Is he going to buy shopping centres, put up apartment buildings or erect a grand mansion? What is this $25 a month going to do for the pensioner? What is it going to enable the older people to do that is so inflationary? Will they buy a little more food or perhaps meet their rent commitments? They may spend it on drugs. Is this inflationary? They might buy a gift for their grandchildren. Would this be inflationary? They might take a trip.
If you study the expenditures of the older people in our society you will find that with few exceptions they are spending their money on fundamental things, and by no stretch of the imagination are those the things that are promoting inflationary pressure in this country. I was disturbed when the Minister of Finance brought in his great budget which was heralded for its originality.

It was original because he adopted a magnificent double standard of taxation to gain the revenues he required. He was quite willing to impose taxes on the individual but when it came to corporations taxes were not the answer. Loans were the answer. I believe these loans amounted to over $300 million, and I believe that amount would meet at least half the cost of increasing the old age pension. Why do we have this double standard? Why was the government not prepared to raise the money and provide an increase in old age pensions?
We talk about national unity in Canada and we regret the fact that our people are increasingly turning to their provincial governments for assistance. We regret the fact that the people have a greater affection for their provincial governments than they have for their national government in Ottawa. Is this surprising when the federal government displays such callousness? If the federal government wants to make a contribution to national unity, if it wants the people of Canada to feel that those who sit here in Ottawa are not insulated from the rest of the people in this country, it should do something about old age pensions. However, the government does not hear the voice of the old age pensioners. So, Mr. Chairman, the provincial governments tell their people that they can do it on their own, that they recognize their need and will raise the pension. [DOT] (3:50 pjn.)
Because those governments are closer to the people is no excuse for inaction on the part of the government in Ottawa. If the federal government in talking of national unity wants to make Canadians from one end of Canada to the other feel as though the government at Ottawa does care about them and wants to do something for them, then let the government act in fields such as this. Let the government at least do something in fields over which they have jurisdiction.
There is no question that the federal government can raise the old age pension. There is no question that this would benefit every Canadian in every part of the country. But the government does not do this. Frequently the government says it would love to do things to promote national unity and to show the nation that the national government is at least as deserving of the affection of the Canadian people as are the provincial governments. Yet they tell the people that these
June 21, 1966

things are beyond their jurisdiction and that they have no say in the matter. The government does have a say in the matter of old age pensions. But what is its answer? The government merely ignores the wishes and the needs of the people of the country.
Again we hear talk about redressing the balance between the rich provinces and the poor provinces. I think there is a real need for correction of the imbalance and to see that the poor provinces in Canada do receive more consideration than has been the case in the past. So the government brings in a measure which has its own built-in means test. The government brings in a measure, the Canada Assistance Plan, which provides that if a province is big, fat and wealthy it will get more money. The more money it can raise the more money it will receive. But if a poor little province cannot raise much money the federal government just matches the amount which is raised.

Mr. Chairman, I have
some observations to make in regard to the subject of social security and in particular in regard to the Canada Assistance Plan, the item we are now discussing. 1 begin by referring to the summary of the minister, reported at page 6407 of Hansard, in which he said:
-the Canada Assistance Plan will provide: a basis for co-ordinating public assistance programs in Canada; -
That has been referred to by the hon. member for Perth.
-federal sharing for the first time in mothers' allowance programs; federal support for the strengthening of administration and welfare services related to social assistance programs; emphasis on developing, improving and extending services designated to lessen the amount of dependency; federal aid for buttressing child and youth welfare services, federal sharing of health care costs for social assistance recipients-
In large measure it is a bringing together, in co-ordination, programs of social security which time and experience have indicated are necessary. As has been stated by the hon. member for Simcoe East and the hon. member for Perth, there is no question whatever that this party will take any stand other than that of support for this legislation. Indeed, the hon. member for Perth set out in detail the course of action taken by the government of which I had the honour to be the prime minister.
I would remind the committee that in addition to the matters to which the hon. member made reference, during our period of office we reduced the residence requirement for payment of old age pensions in Canada from 20 years to 10 years. We brought in for the first time legislation to allow recipients of pensions to take their pensions with them when leaving Canada for health or other reasons. We brought about the increase in pensions, to which the hon. member made reference, from $46 to $65 per month, covering not only old age pensions but also blind persons' allowances and disability allowances. In one other field of social security, that of unemployment assistance, we removed the threshold clause and for the first time Canadians from all provinces in Canada and from the territories were made eligible to receive unemployment assistance benefits.

Canada Assistance Plan
These and other matters, Mr. Chairman, indicate that social security is not a matter of monopoly by any one party. In the field of hospital construction the grants were increased during the six years that we were in office by 175 per cent. Grants for hospital beds used for active treatment were doubled from $1,000 to $2,000. I might deal with many of the changes made to assist those who were in need and to alleviate the economic conditions of those who required assistance.
In other words, we endeavoured to bring about within this nation a wide expansion of social justice, which I might define as the concern of government matched by government action to bring about higher standards of welfare for our fellow men and in particular for those who, because of age, disability, unemployment or other causes, would otherwise not enjoy a reasonable share of the good life.

Very little argument, if any, will come from this side of the house against any suggestion that all Canadians as human beings are entitled to a decent standard of living. This is true particularly of the aged who have served this country well in its development. The Canada Assistance Plan resolution and the bill which will follow will go a long way toward Ailing the gaps that exist in present assistance programs and will help the aged and other disadvantaged groups to live in a more equitable manner than they can at the present time.
One of the big difficulties in respect of assistance programs now in operation is the application of the means test. This is an unfair and unrealistic way in which to provide assistance. Under the provisions of the present means test the income of recipients of assistance includes not only actual disposable earnings but also national amounts, for example, for rent in cases of individuals who own their own homes. Even though a person does not receive a nickel in the way of rent from a property he owns and lives in he must include a certain amount as rent in his income.
The present deffnition of means is unfair to those individuals who have been able to accumulate some savings during a lifetime of hard work. The present level of permissible savings is far too low, and very often because of the length of time required for provincial authorities administering these programs to come to a decision on applications for help these individuals who have accumulated savings below the permissable level must dip into them in order to exist. In this way they deplete these savings while waiting for approval of their applications for social assistance.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
One of the most valuable features of the new Canada Assistance Plan will be the substitution of a needs test for the present means test so that amounts paid can be based on the actual need of the senior citizen the widow, the disabled and the blind who apply. Perhaps some of them may need $100 while others may only need $90 and still others may need $125 a month or more. According to my understanding of the bill which will evolve from this resolution, no limit will be
Canada Assistance Plan put on the amount which the federal government will be able to contribute to match the provincial contributions available under the new programs based on the Canada Assistance Plan to meet the needs of those covered by it.
There comes a time, Mr. Chairman, when measures put forward in an attempt to treat all people in certain categories fairly turn out to have just the opposite effect. There comes a time when measures put forward on this basis actually create inequality. I think it is obvious that needs differ in different parts of the country. An amount that may be adequate in some outport in Newfoundland is unlikely to be adequate in Toronto or Windsor, and in fact needs may differ among people with similar problems living in the same community.
Someone once said that in medieval France the law treated everyone alike; it made it illegal for both rich and poor to sleep under bridges. I think it would be agreed by anyone studying this approach, which still exists under many laws today, that it provides a most unequal form of equality. So, to do nothing more in the Aeld of social security than give people irrespective of need exactly the same amount can and does create and perpetuate inequalities.
I think there is no question that there is need in Canada today for a basic level of social assistance all across the country. However, it is my argument that to continue to give the same across-the-board increases, where the need for such increases exists, to everyone in Canada in exactly the same manner no matter what their individual needs in their areas may be will have the effect of creating and perpetuating inequalities. For example, I suggest that giving $100 a month, as the Conservative party has suggested, to everyone irrespective of their needs and of the amounts they have available will mean giving $100 a month not only to the needy, the aged and others in need of assistance but also to people such as E. P. Taylor and Senator McCutcheon. I suggest that even the good Senator McCutcheon will agree that he does not require this type of help now nor will he need it in the foreseeable future. I do not intend to speak disrespectfully of him, Mr. Chairman.

Others could be mentioned who are quite well off financially and who would receive this assistance although they are quite well able to take care of themselves.
I think the effect of the Canada Assistance Plan will not be to foster inequality but rather create a plan which will meet the needs of the individuals concerned. I might also say, that the use of the flexible needs test approach upon which the Canada Assistance Plan is based will help to bring about a more effective and efficient use of the moneys contributed to the federal government by the taxpayers of this country. It permits greater help to be given to those who are really in need and at the same time it creates a lesser burden on the taxpayer and a more effective use of his tax contributions than might otherwise be the case.
It is important to note that the programs covered by the Canada Assistance Plan are to be administered by the provincial governments because the existing constitutional arrangements of this country give them the basic authority required in this area. I think this is something we have to accept since we have to base federal assistance and support on the constitutional structure of this country.
And I think it is important to note that under this resolution the Canada Assistance Plan enables the provinces to increase their services through the recruitment of social service workers. For the flexible needs test approach to work most effectively it should be administered and applied in a humane fashion by a sufficient number of trained and interested people who are not only concerned with putting in a day's work but with dealing with the human needs of the people who come to them for help.
An important feature of the proposed Canada Assistance Plan is its emphasis on rehabilitation. Many of the aged who will be covered by the plan have contributed to the active life of this country and should therefore be entitled to call upon their fellow citizens to provide them, through federal and provincial assistance, with a decent standard of living with which to complete their days. However, there are others in need of social assistance who, with proper help, rehabilitation and training, will be able to play a more active and more useful role in the life of this country, and I am sure that is what many of them would like to do. I believe that the Canada Assistance Plan will make it possible for them to do so.

As I said at the beginning of my remarks, Mr. Chairman, I understand there will be no limit on the amount of federal contributions to the programs supported by the Canada Assistance Plan provided these will be matched by the provinces. I hope that the provincial governments will not refrain from accepting their share of the responsibilities which at the present time seems to be constitutionally theirs so as to make the Canada Assistance Plan work in the way it is intended to work.
I also think it is an obligation of the provincial governments who will be administering the plan to inform the people who will benefit from it, and their families and neighbours, of the role of the federal government in providing not only the financing but also the framework of the social assistance programs covered by the Canada Assistance Plan. The public has the right to know what is being done with its tax dollars. It has the right to know the reason for these programs and who is paying for them. I urge the minister to make certain, in applying the legislation which we are discussing, that the methods of its implementation will be put into effect in such a way as to make the people of Canada aware of the contributions of the federal government. The provinces also have an obligation to inform the citizens living within their boundaries of the efforts of the federal government in providing a large part of this additional assistance.
I urge this house to support the Canada Assistance Plan and pass this resolution as quickly as possible so that the aged, needy mothers and children, the blind, the disabled and other groups concerned may receive the aid provided under its terms.

I suspect this is the reason the minister backed off from the idea of a guaranteed annual income. It would mean that we would not have the sort of exercise in politics that we have had this afternoon when speaker after speaker, particularly the Leader of the Opposition, indulged in the sort of political display that does not win elections in Canada any longer but only serves to complicate the election picture.
I should like to recall to the members of this committee the Senate report on aging, which is a remarkable report. A week or two ago Dr. Bortz from the United States appeared before a committee and spoke to us on the problems of the aged. He had the highest of praise for this report and said he wished he could claim it for his own country. He gave the Senate committee tremendous credit for its report which brought forth the concept of a guaranteed annual income. I should like to quote a paragraph or two from the report:
If this approach were adopted the following steps would be involved:
1. The establishment of a technically competent body to study the income needs of older people and to develop a socially acceptable minimum budget for single persons and couples, which would be adjusted automatically each year on the basis of a suitable index of consumer spending or of earnings, with a review every five years to reflect changes in the relative circumstances of the working population and the retired population.
Canada Assistance Plan
What a wonderful thing that would be. This country is capable of accomplishing it, we have the machinery. We could get old age security pensions out of the purely political area. The Senate committee made a further elaboration of the program as follows:
(a)	that the only conditions for eligibility under the income guaranteed program be age, as indicated above, ten years' residence in Canada, and net cash income from all sources, including old age security and the Canada Pension Plan, below the above amount.
(b)	that the program be administered and financed by the federal government.
(c)	that the procedure call for the completion of a simplified income form annually and that the amount by which the declared income falls short of the established minima in any year constitute the benefit for the year following.

The one thing it would do would be to remove the idea of a means test and the guaranteed annual income would be accepted as a right. I believe this idea would be acceptable to the elderly people of Canada. I know they have been frightened away from it since the Senate report was made public. I believe they have been so frightened for political reasons because the present system is too valuable to too many people. We know that as long as old age pensions are a political football in Canada no government will be prepared to raise the pension to the point where it should be because if they did they would not be able to use it again, at least not immediately, in the Canadian political picture.
I urge the government to move on the matter of a guaranteed annual income. It must be put into practice somewhere on this continent. It is coming, I know, in many developed countries of the world. Let us lead for a change instead of following. Over and over again in this session it has been said the federal government should show strength. We hear that the provincial governments have been showing the strength. Here is the place for the federal government to try out a new concept, a concept where they have nothing to lose. The elderly people could not be any worse off than they are under the present system.
Once this system was tried I believe the government would find it would solve many problems. I believe the aged would find it acceptable. Then we could go on with this unusual concept and develop it until it became a factor in the lives of the Canadian

Mr. Chairman, I listened very carefully and with great interest to the minister when he was introducing this resolution last night and I noticed a little less

June 21. 1966
Crop Insurance Act
confidence in his remarks than I had noticed in his introduction of previous legislation. When he was speaking he reminded me of a cat walking across the piano keys with the sun in its eyes. I think he indicated quite clearly by his presentation and his manner of delivery that he considers this more or less experimental legislation and that he is not quite certain about its development in the future.
However, Mr. Chairman, we support the principle of crop insurance because we believe it is sound. From our point of view crop insurance for agricultural producers is the counterpart of unemployment insurance for industrial and other workers in Canada. To date, however, it is obvious from the reports we have had with respect to the administration of the crop insurance legislation that farmers have not, shall I say, been very enthusiastic over this legislation to date and have not been attracted by the terms of the legislation or the contracts or agreements required with respect to certain crops in various regions. I think it is quite fair to say that this is experimental legislation which will be developed from experience.
I might say, Mr. Chairman, speaking personally and I think with considerable support in the party of which I am a member, that crop insurance will not be successful until we allow the law of averages to operate by including all farmers in Canada under the legislation so that they may take advantage of it. I hope it will be extended to all farmers. Personally, provided there are proper safeguards I would be in favour of the consideration of a tax to provide crop insurance for all agricultural producers in this country. That is just my personal opinion. I think it would go a long way toward solving the difficulties which have been experienced to date with respect to various groups and various regions and with respect to the different circumstances under which various types of producers operate, because conditions are very varied in Canada.
I do not underestimate the difficulties in developing this type of legislation. I am sure that anyone with any experience in agriculture realizes that it will be some time before we have dominion-wide crop insurance which will be satisfactory to the great bulk of the agricultural producers in Canada.
I was very pleased to hear the minister speak of the conference held with the provincial ministers and of the decisions arrived at as the result of the experience to date. I

think it is necessary that we have close co-operation with the provincial administrators if we want this type of legislation to be successful in the long run. I was interested to note that the minister said that the original 60 per cent coverage would now, as has been suggested, be raised to 80 per cent. I think that is a step in the right direction. I am glad that fruit tree destruction will be covered in future. This has been brought about largely as a result of the experience in the Okanagan where, through quite unprecedented frost, a large number of fruit trees were frozen and the capital investment of the fruit farmers in this respect had to be replaced. I was glad to hear that perennial and other plants will be covered in this new legislation.
The minister mentioned that he had, I think, a few minor amendments to introduce on second reading of the bill. We are looking forward to hearing what those minor amendments are. At any rate, the whole purpose of crop insurance is to reduce the hazards of weather, disease, pests and insects that are faced by all agricultural producers in Canada but by some in greater measure than others. There are certain areas which are, shall I say, high risk areas. There are others where there is very little risk so far as obtaining an adequate crop is concerned.
It might interest you to know, Mr. Chairman, that I have a property where a drop of rain need never fall and yet we have the most bountiful crops. I see the right hon. Leader of the Opposition looking at me speculatively. Let me explain, because it shows how different conditions can be. The ranch is in a valley some eight miles long and about three-quarters of a mile wide. It is covered with a ten foot depth of very fertile black soil which is very productive. The soil is on top of a solid rock basin and the mountains on both sides are between 7,000 and 9,000 feet high. The water in the valley comes from the mountains. Plenty of water comes from the mountains because they have snow on them which melts in the summer months, flows into the valley and down to the basin of rock ten feet below the surface. Then, of course, the moisture rises by capillary action. These are unusual circumstances, and that is why in that valley we only require one acre of land per season to pasture an animal whereas in the prairies 50 or 60 acres of range land are required to do the same thing.
In certain areas, even in the Kootenays, I know that owing to certain local climatic conditions apples produce scab at a much
June 21, 1966

greater rate than in other places. There are so many changes of circumstance and condition with respect to climate and other things that I do not think we should be finally satisfied until we have a crop insurance scheme in which all farmers in Canada are covered. The law of averages ought to be brought into play and crop insurance ought to be envisaged on the basis of a tax.
I shall not say more at this time. We are looking forward to the introduction of the bill. At that time we shall have the opportunity of asking the minister for a further explanation about the administration of the act and about the proposed amendments which have been mentioned and will be before us on second reading.

I have only a few words to say on the introduction of this resolution dealing with the Crop Insurance Act.
First, I must congratulate the minister for taking the initiative of proposing a measure to amend that act. Surly he started out right by consulting, as he did, all the provinces. The job we did on the committee on agriculture, forestry and rural development was useful for the minister in this sense that it helped him draft an act which will finally win the approval of all provinces.
The province of Quebec-it is nobody's se-cre*

did not yet dare undertake such insurance plans. We are always wondering for what reasons. We mentioned in the committee that the main reason was probably the diversity of cultures in Quebec and particularly the removal or the lack of insurance in the case of truck gardening.
Under the old act, truck gardening was not considered insurable. I believe that by adding this clause, the intention is to make insurance available for truck gardening and the main cultures in the province of Quebec. In my opinion, there is no reference to the volume or density of the crop, but simply to each individual farmer's crop.
There were objections because of the rather small volume of certain production classes in the province of Quebec. I do not understand why, when I find, in other provinces, certain classes whose volume is lesser still than in the province of Quebec, the latter would not seek an agreement with the federal government.
I also wish to call the attention of the minister to the fact that the province of Quebec would certainly be interested in a crop insurance which would cover not only damage caused by natural elements, but also damage caused by some artificial elements. Besides natural causes such as hail, frost, drought and parasites, etc., there are also artificial plagues such as we have been visited by for the last two or three years in our areas, specifically, the famous man-made rain.
These damages must absolutely be covered by insurance and, as I pointed out to the committee, in a way that will not be more expensive for the farmers but will have such disasters paid for by those responsible for them; in my area, they are the large lumber
Crop Insurance Act
operators. These people cut their lumber during the summer and must have constant rain on their forests.
I believe this is a very important point to bring up when the minister undertakes discussions with the Quebec agriculture minister. It is a very important point for the province of Quebec, precisely due to the repeated artificial rains every summer. And I feel I should inform the minister that the pressure is being maintained also on the provincial minister.
Farmers' organizations have already started and I have already received a letter from the Catholic Farmers Union on this matter, asking me to call the minister's particular attention not only to the losses incurred from natural causes, but specifically from such notorious artificial devices which have been wreaking havoc with our agriculture.
I hope that Quebec and all other provinces will reach an agreement on the benefits now being offered under the act, that is 25 per cent of the premium payments and 80 per cent of the losses. I trust the provinces will seriously consider this act and will help increase the working capital of this insurance, so that it will be in a position to render the expected services.

Mr. Chairman, I rise to give strong support to this measure because it is going to increase the coverage from 60 per cent to 80 per cent of crop losses and also increase the government's share of payments of premiums from 20 per cent to 25 per cent. Both of these changes are very desirable and necessary.
Such a measure is particularly necessary at a time like this when the farmer's costs are rising and his returns are shrinking every day. The farmer must be assured of a fair return for his crop just as the industrial worker is assured of a fair return for his labour through the efforts of his labour union and through unemployment insurance when by no fault of his own his employment is cut off. As we know, when the industrial worker loses his job through no fault of his own unemployment insurance takes over and he is looked after until it is possible for him to obtain work at a future time. In exactly the same way, when a farmer loses his crop I believe he must be compensated for it adequately through crop insurance.

Mr. Chairman, I have only five or six minutes to discuss some aspects of crop insurance. At the outset I should like to say to the minister that we are in agreement with some of the amendments which we expect to find in the bill following this resolution. First of all, we think a change in the maximum coverage from 60 per cent to 80 per cent is desirable. The minister said there would be some arrangement made with the provinces so that the crop insurance could be calculated on a single farm experience. We will be watching with a great deal of interest how the administration of this works out because I think there has been a lot of pressure on the Department of Agriculture in respect of what they have done under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act in the past.
I should like to say that I appreciate some of the reasons which have been advanced for resisting payment of prairie farm assistance on the basis of a single farm experience. My main reason for participating very briefly in the debate this afternoon is to raise again a question which I have raised a number of times before. Why has the federal Department of Agriculture not used extensively the experience gained under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act over the past 27 years in dealing with payments to farmers who have

lost their crops for one reason or another? I would think there must be a wealth of experience among the large number of personnel who have been involved which could be used beneficially in the administration of a crop insurance program. This may be an academic question now because the federal government has entered into agreements with some of the provinces. It seems they are attempting to encourage the provinces to take part in a national crop insurance program.
I am a little apprehensive about what may happen to the prairie farm assistance legislation in the years ahead. If there should be any disposition on the part of the federal Department of Agriculture to withdraw from the prairie farm assistance program before crop insurance is tried successfully to the point where it is working satisfactorily, particularly in the Prairie provinces, I would point out that we must remember that the Prairie Farm Assistance Act has been a very satisfactory means of taking some of the tragedy out of the major crop losses over the past 27 years. If we consider the operation of that act over the period of 27 years I believe we will find that it probably has been one of the cheapest programs in relation to the number of people who have been guaranteed some return. As I say, taking into account the number of years, the number of farmers and the very large area that has been covered, this is no time to be thinking of setting that act aside until we are satisfied that the crop insurance program has developed to the point where it does in fact meet all the objectives which have been laid out.
The reason I mention this matter at this time is that I have heard rumours that there is some idea that in the near future, depending on what is the definition of "near future", the federal government will be encouraging more areas to get into crop insurance so that it can withdraw from the prairie farm assistance program. I think it would be wrong to move too quickly in this regard until we are satisfied that these other provisions are a satisfactory alternative to the provisions of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act.

speakeroldname: Mr. A. J. P. Cameron (High Park) moved

speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. S-13, respecting Canada Health and Accident Assurance Corporation.
Private Bills
He said: Mr. Speaker, Bill S-13 is a bill respecting Canada Health and Accident Assurance Corporation which was incorporated by special act of parliament in 1945 and has its head office in the city of Waterloo in the province of Ontario. At the time of commencement of business the corporation had a small office and employed a staff of four. Since that time the history of the corporation has been one of steady and progressive growth. It is now a healthy and successful organization, having an administrative staff of 95 and selling its policies through 40 active agencies in all provinces of Canada, using the services of over 300 salesmen. The present number of policyholders of the corporation is in excess of 70,000.
At the present time the corporation offers policies of insurance covering all aspects of medical, surgical and time-loss insurance. The acceptance by the public of the services offered by the corporation is indicated by the annual increase in net premium income. In the first year of its operation the corporation had a net premium income of $73,000. This had grown to $1,608,000 by 1950, increased to $2,830,000 by 1955 and to $3,819,000 by 1960. The year end figure for 1965 approaches $6,000,000.
The last report of the Superintendent of Insurance for Canada discloses that Canada Health and Accident Assurance Corporation is the largest Canadian company engaged solely in the field of accident and sickness insurance. The report further discloses that the net premiums written with respect to individual cancellable policies by all-Canadian companies totalled approximately $7,100,000. Of this amount over $4,500,000 was written by Canada Health and Accident Assurance Corporation.
Based on its past experience, the corporation feels that it can now profitably enter into the field of life insurance. At the time the corporation enters into this field it will be more than able to meet the financial requirements as set out by the Department of Insurance. The corporation has been transacting business in the province of Quebec since 1950 and has increased its net premium income from $160,000 to more than $760,000. As Canada is a bilingual country the corporation feels that it should carry on business not only under the English form of its name but also under the French form, namely, La Corporation Canadienne D'Assurances Santd et Accidents.

June 21. 1966
Private Bills
The corporation also desires to increase its authorized capital stock to $2,000,000, divided into shares of $10 each to satisfy the requirements of the Department of Insurance.
The business of the corporation is presently administered by a board of directors, all of whom are Canadian citizens ordinarily resident in Canada. All shares in the corporation are presently owned by Canadian residents. It is the intention of the corporation to maintain Canadian management and ownership.
The corporation feels that by reason of its past history, progress and development it has indicated its ability to enter successfully into the field of life insurance. The corporation believes that its entry into the life insurance field would afford it greater opportunities to use the Canadian skills and initiative which have given it leadership in its existing fields of endeavour.

subtopic: CANADA HEALTH AND ACCIDENT ASSURANCE CORPORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I know the hon. member for High Park (Mr. Cameron) will be pleased that this bill has finally reached the stage of discussion because he expected it would proceed during two or three past private members' hours but on each occasion some unforeseen development prevented that.
It seems to me that this and other similar bills unfortunately have a political flavour attached to them by reason of the manner in which they are handled. I do not say that with any unkindness to the hon. member, but the system operates in such a way that it is always a member on the government side who is selected to channel bills of this sort through the house. Inasmuch as the original directors of this company were from the city of Waterloo, it seems passing strange that one of the members of parliament representing that area was not chosen to sponsor the bill, thereby giving it a more non-political complexion.
I note that almost all private bills of this kind are sponsored by members on the government side. For some reason or other the promoters gravitate toward government members, perhaps with the idea that greater favours will result. That is an incidental and inconsequential point at this time.

subtopic: CANADA HEALTH AND ACCIDENT ASSURANCE CORPORATION

subtopic: CANADA HEALTH AND ACCIDENT ASSURANCE CORPORATION
speechtext:
I was not referring to page 28 but to the general policy. In the past people in various sections of the house have been chosen to sponsor similar bills but the general trend is for promoters to seek sponsors on the government side.
I am sure that the members of this house, particularly those who have advanced the cause of bilingualism, will look favourably upon at least the first part of the bill by which the company seeks authority to do business under both English and French versions of its name. This company has been doing business in the province of Quebec since 1950 but it did not decide until now that it would be worth while to recognize bilingualism. It is only doing so in this instance for profitable purposes rather than as a real recognition of the bilingual nature of this country.
One of the other aspects of this bill which I think is unique is, as the hon. member for High Park has stated, that all the shares of the company at the present time are owned by Canadian residents. That does not mean that they are owned by Canadian citizens but by people who are ordinarily resident in Canada. This is a step which has been taken as a token attempt to give corporations operating in Canada a nationalistic purpose, namely, to have the directors and shareholders comprised as much as possible of people who are ordinarily resident in Canada.
[DOT] (6:10 p.m.)
It augurs at least partially well for the company that all its shareholders are resident in Canada, and I take the use of the word "resident" to mean that they are not necessarily all Canadian citizens.
This company reflects to a large degree a success story because only some 20 years ago when it first went into business, as the hon. member for High Park pointed out, it employed only four people. I understand that at the present time it employs an administrative staff of some 95 people as well as 200 or 300 salesmen. To increase the sales and administrative staff from a total of four people to half a thousand in a matter of 20 years reflects a large degree of success. The same applies to the income of the company over the same period of time. I believe that this company started operating in 1945 or 1946 and had a net premium income of some
June 21, 1966

Private Bills
$73,000 but in 1965 its income was close to $6 million. This again reflects the success that can be achieved by companies in the insurance field. It also indicates the incentive of this company is solely to make profit, which undoubtedly applies to other companies in the life insurance field.
I am sure this company does not ask to be incorporated simply because its corporate officers happen to think it is a good thing for Canada. In fact, nowhere in the statement of the hon. member for High Park nor in the introductory remarks of the Senator who introduced this bill in the Senate was there even an intimation of any concern for the public good. I am sure the motivation here is the creation of an extremely profitable venture as has been proved by the success of the company over the last 20 years. The company now seeks to expand this success because it realizes how lucrative is the field of life insurance.
The reasoning advanced by my colleague, the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett), on another bill a few weeks ago should serve the house well in considering these matters in the future and should also serve the sponsors of such bills as this because even though they are private bills the companies established under such bills may have a great impact on the economy of Canada. As I have previously said, nowhere in this bill is there any intimation that the good of the country is being taken into consideration in the incorporation of this company.
The only thing this company is saying is that its purpose is to be able to enter into the field of life insurance successfully. It believes that its entry into the life insurance field will afford it greater opportunities to use the Canadian skills and initiative which have given it leadership in its existing fields of endeavour. In other words, the company simply hopes to use the abilities and techniques it has developed over the years to its advantage in the lucrative field of life insurance and the public good can come next, if it is considered at all.
I think that the sponsor of the bill should have considered this aspect and I also think that when this bill is considered in committee of the whole great attention should be given to finding out how the Canada Health and Accident Assurance Corporation will be able to serve the public welfare because this is the basis upon which we should decide to act in this matter.
Here is a company asking parliament to bestow upon it the right to make increasingly greater profits out of the activity of selling life insurance policies. I believe it is simply not good enough to say that the company has been so successful over the past few years, both in terms of increasing staff and increasing profits, that parliament on the basis of that success should give it an opportunity to make even greater profits. I believe we should look a little bit further into the matter.
As I said, this company is asking parliament to set aside consideration of public legislation to deal with its own private affairs. I submit that such matters should be dealt with in another way. We simply cannot continue to deal with these companies by rubberstamping a bill which is presented to us by a sponsor who reads a statement prepared by somebody else. I am not casting any reflections on the hon. member who sponsored this; I am speaking in general of such bills. The statement read by the hon. member for High Park in moving second reading of this bill is almost word for word a repetition of the statement made in the Senate. Maybe the sponsor of the bill will say that he read the statement made in the other place because he thought it was such an overpowering and overwhelming argument that he could not possibly improve it.
This may be true in this case but I have noticed that almost the identical procedure is followed with other private bills. Whatever is said in the Senate is repeated here by the sponsor of the bill. Who knows where the Senator got his information? Presumably he got it from some lawyer in an office in Toronto or Ottawa who is trying to engineer the incorporation of a company. This lawyer is only presenting the favourable aspects of the company. He gives this information to the Senator who reads it into the record of the Senate in substantiation of a bill which he has not really examined at all. In most cases the Senator is only repeating information prepared by a person who is seeking to have a company incorporated. I think this is a one-sided approach. This is what may have happened in this instance especially in view of the fact that the introductory remarks made by the hon member for High Park are almost identical, word for word and comma for comma, with those which were made in the Senate when this bill was considered there on January 23, if my memory serves me correctly.
Private Bills

[DOT] (6:20 p.m.)
This is not nearly good enough because it is just a continuation of the old insurance sales pitch. We all know that when an insurance agent comes to sell insurance, whether he works for Canada Health and Accident Assurance Corporation or any other company, he is only going to tell you what is good about the insurance. He is going to tell you how beneficial the insurance policy will be. He does not tell you about the bad parts. He does not tell you about the loopholes, nor does he explain the fine print. He explains how wonderful everything will be if you just buy his insurance policy. This is the sales pitch that is being used here. Someone comes forward and says how wonderful it will be if we just pass this bill. This is one side of the story.
I believe there devolves upon anyone who comes into parliament and advances a particular idea, especially an idea such as this which can have an influence upon millions of Canadians to the extent of millions of dollars, a duty to give us more than a simple recitation of an explanation developed in a lawyer's office. We have to go a little bit further in our examination of this matter. If this bill had not been brought before parliament we would have a different situation. If we could, as I submit we should, send petitions dealing with this particular class of business activity to a public employee who had been given some criteria and authority to issue letters patent for the incorporation of such companies, then I would say that would be a horse of a different colour. If parliament would set up general guideposts and rules and say to applicants, you must meet these standards before you can become incorporated and conduct this type of business in Canada, then we would be dealing with this matter in a different way.
However, that is not the situation. The situation is that the promoters of the Canada Health and Accident Assurance Corporation have selected the hon. member for High Park to advance their cause in this house. So far the only cause he has advanced in connection with the passage of this bill is an indication that its passage would be most helpful to the Canada Health and Accident Assurance Corporation. Nowhere has there been any indication that the passage of this measure would be helpful to the average Canadian citizen. Nowhere is there any indication that the passage of the bill will result in the introduction of any degree of competition, 
any element of desire on the part of the Canada Health and Accident Assurance Corporation to sell a better class of life insurance, to come up with new ideas or new types of coverage. Nowhere is there any indication that life insurance premiums will be decreased if this company happens to get into the business.
These questions are far too important to be passed over lightly simply because the hon. member who sponsors the bill happens to be a nice fellow. I think he is. I do not have any harsh words for him or his activities in the house. However, we are not legislating here for nice fellows, we are legislating for the Canadian people. Nice fellow as the hon. member for High Park is, I do not believe he is a shareholder in this company and I do not believe he is going to have anything to do with the operation of the company. We cannot, therefore, accept the "nice fellow" approach as being the one which should influence us. We have to look at the company itself. We have to ask ourselves, does it make sense that we should authorize this company to increase its capital from half a million dollars to $2 million? Is it for the good of the Canadian people that the capitalization of this company should be increased fourfold to permit it to engage in a type of insurance business in which it is not engaged at the moment?

subtopic: CANADA HEALTH AND ACCIDENT ASSURANCE CORPORATION
speechtext:
One word only, Mr. Speaker, first of all to congratulate the "Canada Health and Accident Assurance Corporation" for having, at long last, adopted a French name and fallen in tune with the others in acknowledgement of Canada's bilingualism from sea to sea.
Another reason brings me to my feet. The member who spoke before me said that the multiplicity of insurance companies was becoming a threat in the field of life insurance. We can, I believe, forgive him those words: he reasons like a socialist who would only have state insurance. But we, who stand for democratic principles, cannot admit that argument, because a multiplicity of insurance companies which have, like the one mentioned in this bill especially, the necessary capital to do well in business, plainly brings added assets to our Canadian economy. In a democratic economy, it is normal competition that adds to the standard of living and, especially, to the general credit of the country.
