speakeroldname: Hon. A. J. MacEachen (Minister of National Health and Welfare) moved
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare; Minister of Amateur Sport
subtopic: ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES FOR HEALTH TRAINING AND RESEARCH FACILITIES
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-199, to provide for the
June 21, 1966

establishment of a health resources fund to assist provinces in the acquisition, construction and renovation of health training facilities and research institutions.
He said: Mr. Speaker, for the benefit of hon. members I should like to deal with some of the details of the bill which incorporates the matters referred to in my statement of June 14 when I described the original proposals made last July by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson), and which were the subject of subsequent meetings with provincial ministers of health.
It will be recalled that I referred to certain conclusions which had been reached by the conference of ministers in regard to these matters, and I should like to assure the house that the government has been guided by these agreed conclusions in drafting the bill which is before us this evening. Under the bill a special account, to be known as the health resources fund, will be established in he consolidated revenue fund and a sum of $500 million will be credited to that account. It is provided that the payments may be made retroactively to January 1 of this year, and not later than the end of 1980, a 15 year period in all.
The $500 million figure was not an amount taken out of the hat. As I pointed out in my opening statement on June 14, departmental officers visited the provinces prior to the Prime Minister's announcement of the size of the fund, in an effort to ascertain approximate needs as foreseen by provincial governments. We all recognized that such estimates were approximate and subject to considerable refinement, but they gave us at least some clue as to foreseeable requirements.
It was never envisaged that the health resources fund would provide payment in full for the projects coming within the ambit of the bill. In fact when the conference of ministers discussed this aspect of the fund, it was recommended that the contribution of the federal government from the fund should not exceed 50 per cent of reasonable costs of any project. Thus, when we speak of projects to be established with the assistance of the fund, we are not speaking of projects totalling $500 million in cost but of projects of approximately $1,000 million.
While the federal moneys payable in accordance with the health resources fund bill will not exceed one half of the total cost, there is no requirement that the other half must be matched by a provincial government.
Health Resources Fund In fact, health resources funds may be available for up to half the cost of a project, even if the provincial government itself makes no direct contribution. For example, if a private foundation were prepared to finance half the cost of an eligible project, health resources funds would still be available if the project otherwise qualified.
It will be noted that in order to have consideration given to a contribution from the fund, an application must be made to the Minister of National Health and Welfare by the government of a province. As members are aware, under our constitution health training facilities come within the jurisdiction of the provinces. Thus, despite the very substantial contributions which will be made by the federal government, it is considered essential to preserve provincial sovereignty in this area by giving consideration only to those projects put forward by and through provincial authorities. The federal government will not accept projects directly from any individual university, hospital, or establishment for the conducting of research in the health field.
The bill stipulates that no payment may be authorized to be made unless the province making the application has developed a provincial plan covering a five year period. This provision is to ensure that individual projects will not be haphazard but rather will fit into a planned, orderly provincial scheme. Not unnaturally, the bill also requires that the provincial government shall provide the minister with necessary information and make available records and other data concerning the cost of the facilities for which assistance is to be provided.
It will be noted that provision is also made in the bill for joint applications on a regional basis in connection with the Atlantic provinces. The concept of regionalization is particularly applicable where small provinces are concerned. It is reasonable to expect that in some instances, though certainly not in all instances, the provinces concerned may themselves decide to set up a single health training facility to meet the general needs of the region.
The four provinces specifically mentioned in this regard in the bill decided to proceed with such projects on this basis. It will be for these provinces to decide jointly the types of projects for which this regional approach will be used.

June 21, 1S66
Health Resources Fund
The Atlantic provinces received particular attention from the conference of ministers because of the extraordinary needs of that region for health training facilities and the relative lack of fiscal capability to provide these facilities. It was unanimously agreed by the minister of health of all the provinces to recommend to the federal government that a sum of $25 million be set aside for the Atlantic provinces in connection with such projects. This is over and above what the Atlantic provinces are entitled to under the per capita formula.
With regard to the rest of the health resources fund it will be noted that more than half, that is, $300 million, will be allocated on a per capita basis to the provinces, while the remaining $175 million will be available in amounts which may be allocated from time to time by the Governor in Council.
The suggestion that this subdivision in the total remaining funds be made came from the conference of ministers of health. It was based on the belief that, while provincial governments clearly were in need of support for health training facilities within the borders of their own provinces, health training facilities, generally of a highly specialized nature, were also needed to serve purposes beyond the borders of a single province. But of greater importance was the consideration that unallocated funds would still be available when needs were more clearly defined for projects which might be developed later in the life of the fund.
Having regard to these considerations, the conference of ministers recommended that the bulk of the funds should be divided into two parts: first, on a per capita basis to meet purely provincial needs, and the second, to assist in meeting the costs of health training and research facilities designed to meet national needs.
I do not propose to go into extensive detail at this time concerning the method of actually calculating the costs of acquiring, constructing or renovating any building, except to point out the type of costs which will not be included. The health resources fund will not include the cost of land, any amount paid or payable as interest, or any amount paid or payable by the federal government under other arrangements.
It will also be noted that residential accommodation may not be supported out of the

health resources fund. This also was a conclusion arrived at by the conference of health minisiers, but 1 might mention that such accommodation may be supportable under other federal programs.
[DOT] (7:10 p.m.)
Because the health resources fund is, as described in the preamble, intended to assist provinces in the acquisition, construction and renovation of facilities, the question will inevitably arise as to the problem of operating costs. These costs are, of course, not included in this statute, which is designed solely for the purpose of providing capital funds. Nevertheless the government recognizes that the provision of buildings designed for certain purposes will not serve the ends for which the assistance was given unless it is possible to operate these facilities. The problem of such operational costs, however, is one which will of necessity require to be dealt with apart from the question of capital costs.
One of the problems inherent in the provision of operating funds in relation to teaching and educational establishments is the extent to which such funds are interrelated with those designed specifically for education in its broadest sense, including health. This area will still have to be examined by all governments, in collaboration with universities, with a view to reaching some workable solutions.
I believe it is particularly important to note one specific inclusion; the costs of basic equipment necessary for the operation of the health training facility. Obviously such equipment is an essential part of such a facility, without which it would not serve the purpose for which it was designed. Reliance will have to be placed, to a considerable extent, on professional opinion with regard to what, in fact, constitutes this basic equipment.
Reliance on professional opinion will, of course, also be necessary in determining whether the health training facility is of a type which meets the general definition set out in the act, having regard to the purposes of the fund.
Members will be interested to learn of the outstanding co-operation we have had already from the Association of Canadian Medical Colleges, which has given us the benefit of their wise counsel in our efforts to define such elusive facilities as "teaching hospitals", for example. It is my hope and anticipation that we shall be able to continue
June 21, 1966

to have the co-operation which we were so generously given in our early deliberations by such professional bodies as the Canadian Medical Association, the Canadian Nurses Association and the Canadian Hospital Association.
During the last number of weeks I have had a considerable number of requests from other professional associations, as well, all of which have expressed keen interest in participating in the work to be associated with the health resources fund, and requesting representation on the advisory committee, for which provision is also made in the act.
It will be noted that the act makes provision for a health resources advisory committee consisting of 11 members, one to be appointed by each of the provinces under the chairmanship of the deputy minister of national health. The composition of this advisory committee was discussed by the conference of ministers, which gave consideration to the possibility of including professional associations. However, the conference was of the opinion that the committee should be established as set out in the act. At the same time, it was recommended that it should be empowered, as it is so empowered, to establish special committees. These committees would undoubtedly include representatives of professional associations and specialists in relevant fields. The government accepted the recommendation of the conference of ministers in this regard.
Mr. Speaker, I have attempted to give a brief outline of the main points in the bill. It is not a long bill and is relatively simple. Of course, in the clause by clause discussion of the bill I will be pleased to deal with any specific matters that are raised by hon. members.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have listened with some interest to the minister's dissertation in respect of what this $500 million will cover and what it will do. Very briefly I should like to deal with three points. First of all, I should like to ask the minister whether it is proposed that the government, through the National Research Council, will take over all the research? I think this is very important. I feel the government should take over the whole fiscal control of national research. I do not see how the provinces adequately could undertake national research projects. They simply have not the funds.
I should like to go into this a little further and say that last year we spent about $9
Health Resources Fund million on research and covered only 65 per cent of our projects. Of the number of applicants who applied, 115 were turned down. This simply is not good enough. It seems pretty ridiculous that when the United States is spending $1 billion on research we are spending just under $10 million. How can we expect to halt the brain drain that is going on.
In the last report made by the late Dr. Farquharson in 1964 he said that research was woefully weak and falling behind all the time both in buildings and equipment. One of the last appeals he made was that this should be stepped up in an effort to stop the brain drain to the United States. I also should like to state that if we operated on the same basis as the United States, we would have to spend ten times as much, or $100 million. I realize, as does everybody now, that you cannot do this overnight; this is a continuous building-up process which must be programmed. However, until today we have dragged our feet. We are very short on medical personnel; we are short on teachers; we are short on medical schools and we are away down on our research.
Each year during the last five years we have been losing well over 500 doctors a year. When we can spend $10 million for the National Film Board, it seems a bit ridiculous that we cannot spend more than $10 million on research. This simply has to be stepped up. There is no point in building up a health resources fund unless you do this, because you will not get anywhere without research. You will not get competent teachers or staff all the way down.
I should like for a minute to dwell on what the minister had to say about this $500 million over 15 years. I do not know the situation in all the provinces, but I imagine they have similar problems. As I understand it, in the province of Ontario the committee is going to spend $300 million in the next six years and over a 10 year period $500 million. Here, Mr. Minister, you are bringing in a health resources fund in an amount of only $500 million. The provincial government is putting that amount into buildings alone, over ten years. I am not talking about personnel. This is the reason I think the government is away down in its approach to this problem. I do not think you will cover 40 per cent of what is required. This does not include teaching personnel in Ontario but only to plans for the construction of buildings. The minister said nothing whatever about replacement and

Health Resources Fund
the putting in of equipment which today is mighty important.
[DOT] (7:20 p.m.)
This is a very serious drawback in view of the development of heart-lung machines, kidney machines, pacemakers and artificial hearts over the last 10 years-and this is only the start. This type of equipment is being developed and improved every day and it is very expensive. If we are not going to make provisions for the purchase and use of these developments, if we are not going to provide money for research and for training doctors then we are not going to be successful in this program. It is doomed to failure and will destroy the esprit de corps of the medical profession.
In relation to the lack of personnel in the medical field, let me point out that four of our major Canadian medical schools are looking seriously at the shortages in their teachers and in funds for equipment for student training. This is facing them now. The situation is becoming serious. Every province must have similar plans in so far as construction of hospital facilities is concerned. The province of Ontario estimates that it will spend $500 million in the next ten year period by way of capital construction costs-as much as the federal government pumps in 15 years.
The minister said that if private individuals decided to invest in the construction of medical facilities the government would go along on a 50-50 basis. I hope the minister is not suggesting that programs of this type will be taken out of provincial control. If the provinces have not as yet gone along with that idea, how is the federal government going to do so? I hope that he will give us some indication as to how he plans to accomplish his ideas when he speaks again.
The minister made a serious error of judgment in referring to medicare plans. He suggested that a medicare plan would be brought into existence next year, but how can he when he has made little or no plans to alleviate the critical shortage of doctors. Does the minister not think he is cheating the people by promising a medical program which cannot be effective because of the lack of services available, particularly when he considers that premiums will be deducted, and taxes will be collected? I remember other occasions when the public was filched because someone else rushed ahead with plans that could not be put into effect. I am not suggesting the government is going ahead too fast with a medical services program, but it

should have before this time instituted a crash program in our medical schools in order to train the necessary personnel.
I can never understand why in the world our medical schools are closed during the summer when we are so short of doctors. That was not the case during the war, when we were much better off as far as medical personnel were concerned. We have not graduated many doctors per year more than we did following the war years, in spite of the fact that our population has increased by 25 per cent in the same 10 years. Does the minister not think that a crash training program is vital to the success of any national medical services plan? I hope he will discuss this serious situation with the provincial ministers of health in order to find some solution. We have the facilities and the teachers and I think we should go along with the suggestion that medical schools be kept open all year. We certainly will not have enough doctors to carry out this program unless we bring them from England or Europe. I understand that will be difficult because in at least some hospitals in England the staffs have come from outside England.
In conclusion let me say I will discuss some situations at a later stage because I think it is vital that we find solutions to these problems which are inherent in such a national medical plan.

Mr. Speaker, the health resources fund legislation is, in the opinion of the members of this party, of tremendous importance. I do not think its importance has been fully appreciated by the house, if one can judge b>
the interest that was taken in the debate or. the resolution which preceded this bill. Noi do I think its importance has been fully realized by the government, if one can judge by the length of time it has taken to bring down the legislation or by the amount of money which is being provided by it. I do not like to use an old hackneyed phrase, but the fact is the legislation has been brought down too late and the amount of money provided is too little.
The importance of this legislation lies in the fact that this is the basis upon which a successful medicare program can be built. I am not one who thinks that we must wait until every facility is available and all the technicians and professional people have been trained before adopting a medicare plan. The fact does remain, however, that medicare in
June 21, 1966

this country will place a tremendous strain upon our facilities and available personnel.
I had some experience in setting up the first hospital insurance plan in Canada-as a matter of fact, the first on this continent -which came into effect in the province of Saskatchewan on January 1, 1947. For two and a half years we had a crash program for the construction of hospitals. When we could not construct new hospitals we converted old airport and army buildings into temporary hospitals. We also had a crash program for training nurses, x-ray and laboratory technicians, because it was quite apparent that the moment hospital insurance came into effect the number who would apply for hospital care would increase. It was also apparent that once hospital insurance became effective the number of people sent to hospitals by physicians would increase, and that unless we were prepared to handle this increase, which we estimated at 25 per cent, congestion in hospitals would develop.
All these statistics in respect of hospital admissions which had been projected turned out to be reasonably accurate. We estimated that the increase would amount to approximately 26 per cent and my recollection is that in two years it was actually 26J per cent. We estimated that this increase would level off and gradually decline as we caught up with the backlog, and as better pre-operational care was provided, cutting down the length of hospital stay. These projections also proved to be accurate.
We had to make sure that when health insurance in any form came into effect facilities and personnel were available. I remember discussing this matter with Mr. Aneurin Bevan, who established the British health services plan. He told me that they had the same experience, that one could expect in the initial stages a marked increase in demand for services, and that unless we were ready to provide these services we would experience great congestion. There is bound to be some congestion with the very best of medical plans in the initial stages, but that congestion can be ameliorated somewhat by a crash program to provide facilities and trained personnel.
[DOT] (7:30 p.m.)
To my mind the tremendous importance of the legislation which is now before the house lies in the fact that the effectiveness of medicare will largely depend upon the legislation which I hope the house will pass very
Health Resources Fund shortly. It will also depend upon the aggressiveness with which the federal Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Mac-Eachen) and the provincial ministers of health make use of the funds provided, so that when medicare is implemented in Canada the people who expect to get those services will be able to avail themselves of them. Nothing would give medicare a greater black eye than for us after July 1, 1967, to say that medical services of all types were available to the people of any given province, and then for those individuals who required medical care to find there were no adequate facilities or sufficient personnel to give them the care to which by law they were entitled, and to which they had contributed financially. Therefore it is of tremendous importance that this program to increase facilities and training and to make available personnel be pushed forward with all possible speed. That is why I said that I think the legislation has been much too late in coming.
It is now two years since the publication of the Hall Commission report. That commission recommended that within six months of receiving the report the government should convene a federal provincial conference and immediately begin to plan the expansion of health facilities and the training of health personnel so that when medicare became a fact it would be an effective program which would make available to the people of this country the services which they were led to expect. I can see no reason why this legislation which is before us now could not have been here a year ago. It is inconceivable to me that one year has not been sufficient for the government to digest this report, to consult with the provinces and to place before the house legislation of the nature which is before us at this time. Instead of that, two years have gone by. If the government keeps its commitment of setting up medicare in Canada by July 1, 1967, the provinces will be left with not more than 12 months to get ready for one of the greatest health experiments ever attempted on the North American continent. As a matter of fact, in some cases the provinces may still have to wait for their provincial legislatures to meet this fall and give them the necessary authorization and financial resources to co-operate in this program.
I am concerned about how the provinces will be able in 12 months to do the job that has to be done. It may be that some of the provinces have anticipated this situation and

June 21. 1966
Health Resources Fund
have already outlined plans and begun programs. I certainly hope they have, because under no circumstances do I want to see any delay in implementing medicare. I want to see it start on July 1, 1967. I can think of no finer centennial project for Canada than that on the anniversary of our 100th birthday we will make medical services available to every citizen of Canada, irrespective of who he is and irrespective of his financial ability to pay. But it will not be easy to do it when the provinces and the various educational institutions have such a short time to meet the heavy demands which will be laid upon them.
I will not belabour the point; it is not much use crying over spilled milk. But I do want to say to the government that I fear the 12 months delay may be very costly, and the congestion which may take place in some provinces when medicare is first set up will be due in no small measure to the fact that this legislation was so late in coming before parliament.
Not only do I think it is late in getting here, but I must say to the minister that I think the amount of money provided is pitifully inadequate.
I know that $500 million sounds like a very large sum of money, but spread over 15 years it comes to an average of some $33 million a year and in my opinion this sum will not begin to carry out the program which was suggested by the Hall Commission. As a matter of fact, on the basis of the information the minister has just given us, that $175 million will be set aside to be spent as the governor in council decides, and $25 million will be set aside for the Atlantic provinces -with which I thoroughly agree-this leaves some $300 million to be spent on the regular run-of-the-mill program which, if you spread it over 15 years, comes to about $20 million a year.
Now let us look at what has to be done. I just want to mention a few of the things which the Hall Commission pointed out will be absolutely imperative if we are to provide the Canadian people with the services they are entitled to expect, once medicare becomes a fact in Canada. First of all they point out that we will need a program to build six new university medical schools as well as expanding the existing medical schools. They point out that by 1971 we will require an additional 7,100 trained doctors. This will necessitate a tremendous program of training, and the construction of six new university medical

schools and the expansion of existing ones will require very large sums of money.
Nothing in the educational field today is as costly as the building of medical schools, because of the equipment and the highly technical apparatus now required in medical schools. The expense is fantastic, and there is no use training doctors unless we are going to give them the very best kind of medical training available, not only because they need it but also because the Canadian people deserve it.
The report of the Hall Commission says that we will also have to build four dental schools and that by 1971 we will have to add 2,130 newly trained dentists to those who are now practising that profession in Canada. Probably one of the biggest tasks will be the job of building 10 new university nursing schools to train the 42,000 additional nurses who will be needed by 1971 if this program is going to provide the services which the Canadian people will expect from it.
[DOT] (7:40 p.m.)
Now, in addition to the medical schools, dental schools and university nursing schools, there are suggestions for local services which will be required, particularly in the rural areas. Suggestions have been made for medicine depots, nursing stations and, very important in a large country like Canada with a sparse population, an air ambulance service. I am sure the minister will agree with the position taken by the Hall Commission, that people in the isolated areas and in rural districts of Canada have a right to expect the same high standard of medical care as will be enjoyed by people in the metropolitan areas. They cannot get that unless there are facilities, first of all, to provide them with emergency care by local medical depots and nursing stations, and then an air ambulance to take them to the large medical centres where they may get the very best of medical and surgical care available.
After all, it is not possible to have a highly trained doctor or group of doctors and surgeons in every community. However, the very least we can do is see that people in isolated communities can be flown quickly and inexpensively to a place where there is a team of medical experts to provide them with the very best surgical and medical care. This is going to cost money, and it is going to cost a great deal of money. I do not believe this $20 million a year will cover the cost.
June 21, 1966

Then, there is the whole question of allied health services which will have to be provided under medicare and for which we have nothing like a sufficient nun . r of trained personnel. I am referring to x-ray technicians, lab technicians, physiotherapists and all the allied technicians that have now become an integral part of the practice of good medicine. Finally, as has been mentioned by the hon. member for Simcoe East (Mr. Ry-nard), the fundamental stimulant for any good medical program is medical research. This country must be prepared to spend very large sums of money, first in building medical research facilities and then in the actual research itself.
When the members of this party speak of medicare, Mr. Speaker, we are not just concerned with transferring the payments from the patient to a government agency. That is only a part of the value of medicare. The other great value of medicare is that it can make possible a much better qual ty of med -cal care; it can provide opportunities for group practice. It can provide opportunities for doctors to take refresher courses. It can provide opportunities lor research and the transmission of the results of that research to the practising professions. If medicare is going to be what we hope it will be, and give to the people of Canada the health er ces 'h need, without any financial obstacle standing between them and the members of the heahn profession, then it will also have to be a program which will give the people the very best kind of health services.
My conviction is that when medicare becomes fully operative in this country it will finally reach the stage wher - the major e '-phasis will be on the practice of preventive medicine. The real aim of a medica c s program is not just to get people well after they are sick, but to keep them from getting sick by developing clinics, group practice and by establishing a close relat on -hip between patients and doctors. When this condition prevails, the average family can go reguiariv to the family physician and, if they require it, be referred to specialists to help (hem keep in good health. This procedure makes possible the diagnosis and early identification of diseases that could later prove serious or even fatal.
I just cannot believe, Mr. Speaker, that the sums of money the minister has been talking about this evening will be anywhere nearly adequate to carry out the vast program that needs to be undertaken. I hope the minister
Health Resources Fund will tell us, either when he concludes this debate or in the committee of the whole, whether these sums of money are to be paid out to the provinces on an annual basis, provided they qualify for them, or whether the federal government will match the projects completed in the provinces on a 50-50 basis, without any regard to the annual allocations. If the $300 million is to be held down to $20 million a year, and if the $175 million which is set aside for special projects is to be allocated on an annual basis, then I suggest to the minister that in my opinion the goals that have been set by the Hall Commission as to the number of doctors, dentists, nurses and allied health services personnel which will be required by 1971 will not be reached.
I hope the minister will say to the universities, medical schools, dental schools and nursing schools, "This is the goal we have for 1971 and you can proceed as fast as you want. If you complete it in two or three years, if you complete it before 1971, we will meet half the costs on the basis of the terms laid down in this legislation." The worst thing that could happen would be for the government each year to dole out this money in annual allocations, and then tell a province or university that has started out with great enthusiasm, "We are very sorry, but we have used up the allocation for this year; you will have to be paid out of next year's allocation."
[DOT] (7:50 p.m.)
That would slow down the whole program. As a matter of fact, this $500 million can, in my opinion, be spent over the next five or seven years-never mind 15 years. As a matter of fact, it will have to be spent over a much shorter period than 15 years if it is going to do the job which has to be done. Otherwise we will have a medicare program which will be hampered and hamstrung from the very beginning, owing to a lack of facilities and personnel.
I want to express my complete support for the position taken by the hon. member for Simcoe East (Mr. Rynard), who said that what the situation calls for is a crash program. I think that not only the federal government but the provincial governments will have to show the kind of imagination and drive that characterizes a real emergency. If we must have, as the Hall Commission suggests, 7,100 more doctors trained in the next five years, then we may have to change the techniques and make it possible for medical schools to operate 11 months in the year. We

June 21, 1966
Health Resources Fund may have to pay bursaries to medical students, and make provision for students allowances. Instead of having to go out and work in the summer months this might enable the students to study throughout the entire year.
We did this sort of thing during the war. We trained doctors because they were needed for the armed services. Many of those doctors are still practising today. I think it would be a brave and somewhat imprudent individual who would suggest that they were not well trained, merely because the courses they undertook were crash courses. We trained many fine doctors, dentists and psychiatrists as a result of those programs which were instituted during the war.
Mr. Speaker, we are just not going to get the doctors, dentists, trained nurses, x-ray and laboratory technicians and the physiotherapists we need if we simply follow the same routine course. We must make it possible for bright and promising young people to leave behind them the normal channels of university entrance, attending university for six or seven months and then working for four months or so, and we must enable them to go into crash courses, with the federal and provincial governments paying their funds and providing their training, as well as giving them a decent living while they take their courses, so that they will be trained as quickly as possible.
I am sure that if we put that kind of challenge to the young people of this country we will get a response. There are thousands of young people in Canada who would like to go into the health profession. In many cases they lack the opportunity and they lack the necessary funds. Everyone knows that one of the most expensive university courses is a medical course. This makes it difficult for all kinds of young people who come from families of modest means to become doctors, dentists or psychiatrists. But if the federal and provincial governments are prepared to embark upon a crash program, the necessary personnel would be available when medicare comes into operation. They will certainly be available when the flood tide has reached its crest. If we start medicare on July 1, 1967 it will reach its crest in 1968 and 1969, the period when there will be the greatest demand. By 1971 it should be starting to level off a bit.
I hope that the minister will not consider that I am harping on some of the defects which I think exist in the government's program. I think that the minister deserves a

good deal of commendation for the persistence and aggressiveness he has shown in pursuing this matter since he assumed the portfolio of National Health and Welfare. I can assure him that we in this party are thoroughly behind him as he presses on with this matter.
Let me also tell him that in our opinion he ought not to be dissuaded from proceeding with medicare on July 1, 1967 because of the problems that will undoubtedly face both him and the provincial governments with reference to provision of facilities and personnel. I am sorry that we did not start making plans sooner; but the fact that we did not start sooner ought not to be made an excuse for delaying the implementation of medicare.
I am sure that all of us have had the experience that, once we have started a program, the pressure of events compels us to move at an accelerated rate to do what has to be done. If we wait until we are absolutely sure that everything is ready before we launch medicare, then we will never start it. Therefore I urge the minister not to delay the setting up of a medicare scheme because of the difficulty of supplying the required facilities and personnel.
Nevertheless, Mr. Speaker, I would point out to him that the best way to make medicare work and the best way to save both himself and the provincial ministers of health a lot of headaches is to make sure that crash programs are devised within the next few weeks, that they are put into operation this fall, and that the money which is being made available by this legislation will be given to the provinces, not on an annual allocation basis at all, but made available to the provinces just as fast as they are able to complete the projects they want to undertake.
I feel sure, Mr. Speaker, that if that course is followed, and if the government is prepared to set up crash training programs, then the minister will get the support of the people of the country, the support of the young people who want to train for the health professions, and I think he will get the support of most of the ministers of health. If he gets that support and if he implements a medicare plan, I am convinced he will be taking one of the great forward steps in the social history of Canada. The minister will have won for himself a place of distinction in the country by having helped to launch a program that will be of inestimable value, not only to the people of our day and generation but to Canadians for all time to come.
June 21, 1966

speechtext:
At
the outset I should like to congratulate the Minister of National Health and Welfare upon the introduction of this measure. It may be said that it is easy for a supporter of the government to do this; but, as the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) stated, the minister is to be commended for his persistence in adhering to the date set for the medicare program and for the establishment of a health resources fund to assist the universities and the hospitals to train staff for medicare and for general purposes
June 21, 1966

throughout the country. I compliment him and I hope the members will agree to pass the bill after scrutinizing it. I have some questions to ask about it myself and I intend to raise them when we come to the clause by clause study of the measure.
May I refer to the brief called Medical Research in Canada-An Analysis of Immediate and Future Needs, which was presented to the government back in January. This is a comprehensive presentation drawing attention to the problems we face today in this field. Incidentally, I am happy to see among the endorsers of this report three eminent doctors, all of McMaster University in Hamilton-J. R. Evans, Principal, College of Health Sciences; W. B. Spaulding, Associate Dean, Faculty of Medicine; and W. J. Walsh, Assistant Dean, Faculty of Medicine.
It is not possible to separate medical research from the university training of scientists, doctors and medical teachers. The message of this brief is clear and simple: Unless support for medical research is increased beyond the level we now envisage, Canadian medical schools will deteriorate and so will the quality of health care provided to the Canadian people.
Not only has the quality of medical care and research work failed to keep pace with that of other highly developed countries but we are also falling behind on a quantitative basis. Today in Canada we have one doctor for every 870 citizens. Twenty countries in the world have a better ratio than this. In order to maintain our present ratio we have to register 1,300 new doctors every year. Our Canadian medical university schools turn out only 850 annually and we are holding our own by bringing in doctors from other countries at the rate of 450 a year, as the report states.
I realize the minister is not dealing with operational costs at the present time. However, the report says that federal government grants for operating expenses of medical research must reach a minimum of $80 millions annually by 1970. The present annual figure is $15 millions. The comparable figure in the United States is $1.3 billions a year. This illustrates how far behind we have fallen in medical research in this country. It will readily be understood why we are losing some of our best medical scientists to the United States. Indeed, this is one of our principal problems.
I agree with many hon. members that federal assistance in this field is of national
Health Resources Fund importance. This question of medical standards has to be considered nationally; unless this is done we shall fall still further behind. I believe the establishment of a health resources fund is one step toward improving a situation which has been allowed to deteriorate.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
Unless we are able to provide sufficient funds we shall not be able to catch up at the pace we would like, and will continue to fall behind. I must agree with other hon. members that the $500 million is not going to be sufficient, especially since only $300 million will be distributed for construction grants and capital grants to universities over a 15 year period.
We lag in scientific research in all fields. I believe, as these doctors say in their brief, that we must give priority to medical research on the grounds that the nation's health is at stake and the demands of the medical profession simply cannot be met at the present scale of our medical research. In their brief the doctors estimate that as many as one third of our Canadian medical schools do not meet U.S. standards. The summary of their brief states this:
Medical research is essential to the provision of high standards of medical education, health services and health care. This fact must be recognized in any programs aimed at broadening health services and raising health care standards in Canada.
We learn from this brief that it takes eight to ten years to plan, build and recruit staff for a new medical school, and a further eight to ten years for its graduates to become trained teacher-scientists to staff other new schools. It also states that this has serious implications for possible future emigration of physicians from Canada to the United States.
At present in the city of Hamilton, McMaster University, after some local problems of land acquisition have been settled, is planning to proceed with a modern complex costing $100 million, to be built by 1980, with the $40 million core of the project to be commenced almost immediately, containing a 400 bed hospital, research units and facilities for allied sciences, all forming part of the modern concept of a research centre and training hospital.
McMaster University is today leading in medical isotope research, with the aid of the nuclear reactor it has on campus, and the provincial government has approved this new $100 million complex. It is a vital necessity, and the Hall commission report has referred

June 21, 1966
Health Resources Fund to it. In fact the description "crash" could be applied to the project itself. What can we do with $300 million when it is realized that here is one new medical research complex that is going to cost $100 million, and this without the acquisition of land required for future expansion?
When a medical school is being constructed and land has to be acquired for that purpose, why should not the cost of that land be included in the over-all cost of construction? Where a university has sufficient land on campus to satisfy its needs, then that is a different matter, but in this instance McMaster University has to acquire land, and that should be taken into consideration. I would ask the minister to consider this matter.
I realize that the provinces have to be consulted, but again I repeat that land acquisition costs should be included in the over-all cost. Under this bill we are simply talking about capital construction costs. There still remain to be provided laboratories and their equipment and facilities. The sum of $300 million is not going to be sufficient, especially when one considers the present crash program being undertaken with respect to medical schools by the province of Ontario. We have a need for money to provide scientists, medical teachers, doctors and physicians to meet the requirements of our expanding population.
But the over-all situation augurs well, and I compliment the government and the minister upon introducing this legislation. It is a first step, and once the plan is approved the government should consult with provincial health ministers with a view to increasing the amount of money in the fund to take care of crash programs, such as the one I have mentioned in connection with McMaster University.
I use McMaster as an example, not because it is situated in Hamilton or because it is expanding its present medical facilities, as is the case with the University of Western Ontario and McGill. This is a case where a completely new complex is being constructed, and when it is completed Ontario will have one of the finest medical complexes on the North American continent.
Unless the federal government is prepared to contribute immediately sufficient funds for this complex the full burden is going to be placed on the provincial government. Providing 50 per cent of the capital cost is quite a contribution, but $300 million is not going to
be sufficient to provide the medical research facilities which are required, particularly if one takes into consideration the brief which has been presented to the government.
I do not intend to speak at length about this new complex at McMaster University, but I should point out that it will include not only the 400 bed hospital but also provision for allied sciences, such as a department of life sciences, a department of psychology, a department of rehabilitation, a diagnostic and treatment centre for out-patients, a school of dentistry, and a family practice centre to be added in the future, something of an innovation in Canada whereby doctors will be allowed to have their offices on campus and have the various laboratories and research facilities available to them.
In the modern concept of medical education there should be an integrated campus covering all the allied sciences such as biochemistry and full laboratory facilities to cover everything else, as well as a nursing school and all other facilities. Mr. Speaker, I keep emphasizing the need for sufficient money to build modern medical complexes. Today we have a serious shortage of medical scientists and teachers in Canada. The government is to be commended on the fact that over a year and a half ago it made a substantial grant to the University of British Columbia for medical research facilities. But that was only a start; we have to move ahead. I agree with other hon. members on the need for a crash program.
Although provinces have jurisdiction over education in medical schools, I personally would have liked to see provision in this bill whereby moneys could be payable directly to a university, once the province has approved the complex that is to be constructed. However, since that is not the case I think it should be made clear that capital cost grants alone are not the answer. Operating costs are very important. Over a long term they become more substantial than the capital costs.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
So although, as the minister stated, he is not dealing with that at this time, I do sincerely wish to bring to his attention again that the cost of the land is a factor when a university or a hospital has to acquire land to build, which is the case I understand in connection with this medical complex at McMaster University. Our universities and hospitals have a major part to play in the
June 21, 1966

planning and development of medical research in Canada. As we move along in this field I think we must look even more closely at what financial aid the federal government is going to undertake in respect of medical schools and medical research facilities, because the important thing is the federal government still is the prime mover with regard to a national medical standard. Unless the federal government takes on this burden then we are going to fall back further and further. We cannot allow that to happen, and I do not think it will happen. I believe the government has taken the right step.
The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) stated it is a year too late. However, I am sure that as a former provincial premier he realizes the number of discussions which have taken place on the matter of federal-provincial co-operation. That, however, is a minor matter. I think this is a good measure. I feel sure it will receive the support of the house, because we in Canada badly need the greatly increased facilities which will be provided by the use of this money, in the training of more doctors, dentists, nurses, and technicians. This will make possible the operation of the greatly expanded health insurance programs which will be coming into existence here in Canada in the months and years ahead.
The only fault which I can find with this measure is that I believe the $500 million which will be provided over the next 15 years is going to turn out to be completely inadequate. Over a 15 year period this averages out to a yearly expenditure of only $33 million a year. As the hon. member for Simcoe East (Mr. Rynard) pointed out when

the construction of buildings and the purchase of equipment. All these things are required in order successfully to provide adequate national medical service.
There is no need for me to repeat the arguments that have been so well advanced by previous speakers but I rise to emphasize one particular angle and to bring it to the attention of the minister. I do so because I am particularly interested in local participation in government sponsored plans wherever possible.
I come from a community that has done a great deal as a result of local effort and sacrifice. I might say that I have had some experience with the recruitment of doctors. I was one of a committee of three who recruited our first doctor, who was a gentleman who had lost his licence in Ontario. Fifty five years ago we persuaded him to come to our community and we promised him the job as bartender of the local saloon as a foundation for his security. He practised medicine for very small fees, sometimes just for a chicken, vegetables or whatever he might have needed. We made one other stipulation: He had to play the organ in the village church on Sunday night.
I may say that we were very glad he got his licence back when he joined the army in company with the hon. member for Kootenay West. In times of war the authorities overlooked past records. I have also had experience with hospital administration, and I helped to establish the first hospital in our district. I was the director of that hospital for 22 years and the president for several years, and I know what it is to establish and run a hospital in the backwoods as the result of local community effort.
We did establish a hospital in that area and we have a hospital today. This is a community with less than 1,000 people and the hospital is valued at something over $22,000. It has excellent bed services, x-ray equipment and modern operating facilities. Only the very serious cases in that area have to be taken a distance of approximately 100 miles to a larger centre. I pay tribute to the doctors and nurses who have worked in this hospital throughout the years. All of this was done as a result of local participation, local effort and, in many cases, local sacrifice.
When we have government sponsored programs, particularly in respect of health insurance or medicare plans, there is a tendency for local participation and interest to decline. I have seen this happen in recent years. I
Health Resources Fund simply rise at this time to bring this fact to the attention of the minister, because it is unfortunate when we do not have continued interest and participation in communities in support of local hospitals.
In connection with this program I urge the minister that everything be done to promote local interest and participation through a good public relations approach, and possibly as a result of the provision of information to local hospital boards in communities throughout the country. I am speaking from my lengthy experience in a small community, but I think the same applies to the towns and larger centres.
[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
I will say this, Mr. Speaker, that people are not as happy today in the affluent society in Canada as they were in the pioneer days. You will ask why. Because many of them have no purpose in living and no direct interest in the society around them. The more local participation we can get in all these projects, the more successful they will be. I simply rise to bring this to the minister's attention. In view of the fact that possibly he has a somewhat similar background to mine, although probably on a more affluent level-anyway he has had similar experiences to mine-I do hope he will duly consider this aspect of the problem and get local people to co-operate with the provincial authorities and the federal government in securing for this development of health services in Canada the success it should have with our human and natural resources.

June 21/ 1966

Health Resources Fund
The hon. member mentioned 21 days. It seems to me that this is unreasoned optimism, in view of the fact that the guide line of 60 days on which the government operated previously has fallen by the wayside quite recently. Much has been said about the need for various types of personnel. Reference has already been made by other hon. members to the need for dental and paramedical personnel. This bill points out the necessity of constructing buildings and providing them with equipment. Is this enough? I do not believe it is. You can build a barn but if you do not have cows to put in it you cannot set up a dairy business. I do not believe that by simply constructing buildings and placing wonderful equipment in them you will automatically provide better medical care and


will automatically get people to stall these buildings.
As has been pointed out by the Canadian Medical Association in the brief at a conference to which I have referred previously:
It is currently observable that certain institutions already built are unable to be used to their full potential because of the lack of trained personnel to operate them. Bricks and mortar are important but the supply of personnel is equally important.
There is laboratory space now available in Canada and not being used. I have already mentioned in this house that in my home city of Saskatoon the University Hospital, which is a very modern hospital, last summer had to close some of its wards which were waiting for patients because there was no personnel available to staff those wards. I believe that if this bill does not provide for an increase in personnel, another bill should be drafted which will provide the incentives mentioned by the hon. member for Northumberland (Mr. Hees), incentives not only for those living in rural areas but to bring back to this country and keep here the type of medical personnel that we will need.
I do not think it is good enough to say that as it is the responsibility of the provinces to look after health and welfare it is they who should come up with a plan. Mr. Speaker, we have before us a bill providing for the establishment of a health resources fund to assist provinces in the acquisition, construction and renovation of health training facilities and research institutions. The purpose of this bill is to attract an increasing number of competent persons to the study and practice of medicine and medical support occupations.
Mr. Speaker, this bill is, in my opinion, another indirect interference in the field of education connected, in the spirit of this bill, to medical training. The new Quebec government is opposed to such an interference on the part of the central government. That is why I suggest, in order to prevent conflicts and tensions prejudicial to the country and

to national unity, to postpone the passing of this bill, so as to allow the new Quebec government to look into it and meet the central authorities in order to agree on terms and conditions.
Anyhow, this attitude of the province of Quebec is not new. During the last federal-provincial conference, the minister of health, Mr. Kierans, speaking on behalf of the province of Quebec of three essential conditions for co-operation in a field as ticklish as this said:
The creation of this fund is acceptable on three conditions.
First of all, money must be granted per capita; secondly, the Quebec government will be the only one having authority to ask and receive money from the fund; thirdly, the Quebec government itself will decide upon its use.
Mr. Speaker, according to the bill the central government reserves the right to distribute at its discretion, and by order in council, a great part that is $125 million of the fund of $500 million. Well, Mr. Speaker, the Quebec government, prior to June 5, 1966, and the new government, are absolutely opposed to this arbitrary way in which the central government will distribute, at its own discretion, a substantial part of this fund intended for health training facilities.
That is another example and even if I am one of the few who speak in that spirit in the house, I will do it until my term expires. Even if sometimes that attitude might bring a smile to the lips of the government members from the province of Quebec, we will see in the years to come who will have the opportunity to smile in this house and who will be wearing slippers at home after the next federal election.
Those problems, Mr. Speaker, must not be solved unilaterally, with that attitude, which I would call indifference and even arrogance towards the opinion of certain provinces and that of the province of Quebec, of always carrying the initiatives of the central government into exclusively provincial fields of jurisdiction.
Personally, when I observe the present government interfering in all the fields of Canadian activity, I cannot see any further reasons for having a Canadian constitution in this country and talking about a federative system in Canada. We have gone beyond that, following all those activities in the manifold details of Canadian life. The needs are great and several hon. members explained airily, with a great display of knowledge, that in the field of medical training
June 21, 1966
and research the needs are urgent and necessary. I agree that those needs exist and that the central government takes an interest in those problems and needs, but according to the Canadian constitution and under a federative system, it is not all justified to interfere in those problems, to engage in the game of "one-upmanship" with the provinces, to keep the larger share of the fiscal cake in Canada and to prevent the provinces from assuming their own responsibilities.
Are the provinces considered mentally retarded in that particular field since we are talking about health? What competence does the present government give the provinces, what intelligence does it grant to the administrators of the ten provincial governments? In the last few weeks or even months, we have had the impression that the present Liberal government is not giving credit for any intelligence to the administrators of the ten provincial governments, does not have enough confidence in them to allow those people to assume their responsibilities. It will be said that such and such a province did not assume a particular field of responsibility, did not take any initiative; it is very easy to understand because the central government, pretexting wars and economic crises, collected all the revenue from taxes in Canada and refuses to give back to the provinces their share of the taxation field.
How could the provinces, British Columbia, Nova Scotia or any other, including Quebec, have enough money to establish these very Health Resources Funds intended for training facilities, when the central government, like Scrooge, like a jealous and all-powerful Croesus, is keeping in its treasury three quarters of Canadian tax revenue? There lies the problem. It is regrettable, Mr. Speaker, that members from the province of Quebec, fully aware of the views and aspirations of their fellow-citizens and of their province rise only to flatter their government. I predict that, some day, they will be appointed ministers, parliamentary secretaries, or sent on marvelous journeys around the world. But they are not fulfilling the mandate entrusted by the Fathers of our Canadian Confederation to us all legislators, until we amend the Constitution, and calling upon us to respect the principles of federalism and the responsibilities of the central government as well as of the provincial governments.
I am not surprised to see some members opposite smiling, or laughing their heads off.

Health Resources Fund I know that people in some quarters are not giving a rap about the aspirations of certain Canadians and of a certain province; but they may realize later on that by keeping the lid on Canadian federalism, and striving towards a unitary system, they will bring about severe conflicts in Canada and the responsible ones will be the very people who kept their eyes shut or who, ostrich-like, stuck their heads in the sand.
I have here the text of the 1867 Constitution, and I dare any member in the house, as well as the hon. minister, to tell me under what provision of the Canadian Constitution, which will remain in force until we amend it, the central government has the right to interfere in the field constituting the substance of this bill.
On the contrary, the object of this bill comes under the exclusive jurisdiction of the provinces as, in 1867, all local, regional, civil, professional, social and educational questions were assigned exclusively to the provinces, under a stipulated compact, within a confederative pact. And neither a province nor the central government has the right to change the agreements accepted at that time, in order to meddle in various fields.
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
Here is an opportunity for centralization rampant in Ottawa. And it is nothing new. For instance in 1919, Ottawa began to meddle in the health field, in social questions, by the passing of an act to contribute to the fight against venereal diseases and to create a public health department, although health and the social field belong to the provinces.
In 1942, Ottawa went even farther into the social and educational field of vocational training. In 1944, it set up the Department of National Health and Welfare. In 1948, it adopted a national program of health and hygiene by providing 13 subsidies. And today, it forges ahead in medical training, adding to the increasing centralization of powers and taxation in Canada which has been the only cause of dissension and misunderstanding between Canadians from Halifax to Vancouver.
Here again this evening we have another example of what is referred to, in fashionable circles, as co-operative federalism, that milk-and-water creation; instead of following the dictates and fundamental principles of true

June 21, 1966

Health Resources Fund federalism, the main principles of which were included in our Canadian constitution, people talk of co-operative federalism to excuse the trespassing, the meddling in exclusively provincial spheres of jurisdiction. We are told that the central government will reach agreements and co-operate with the provinces, and so, we will solve the country's problems. But see how this is done, Mr. Speaker. The central government, moved by a spirit of arrogance and domination, penetrates unilaterally, in a given field, without the ultimate and complete consent of the provinces, or at least that of Quebec, invades a given field, and having moved in, tells the provinces: See, that is what we can do. And out of the funds it distributes, it can allot $175 million, if it so wishes, by order in council, and as it sees fit, to a field of provincial jurisdiction.
Mr. Speaker, newspapermen and public figures were right in saying that this cooperative federalism is just another excuse to justify more unrestrained centralization of powers and authority for the benefit of the federal government and that this amounts to centralization by agreement. It is nothing else, Mr. Speaker. Ottawa trespasses in an area outside its jurisdiction and when it is installed, it plays the liberal, the generous, the debonaire; the central government even plays Santa Claus by making offers right and left to the provinces and saying: Here, we have the money, because we have decided to give you this and that.
Mr. Speaker, here is another bill that will increase the mistrust and misunderstanding between Canadians and in spite of the rumblings I can hear, I challenge their authors to rise, even with the sarcastic smile showing on their faces, to show me in the constitution of Canada, the legality of this bill which is precisely contrary not only to the letter, but to the very spirit of the Canadian constitution.
I know that my own solitary intervention may be unilateral, but this will not prevent both sides of the house from maintaining this centralizing regime because it is based not only on rights but on needs. But, if within six months to a year, fundamental pressures or conflicts unfortunately occur- that would be cruel for the country-the responsibility for such tensions and conflicts will not rest with the province of Quebec but with those who, indifferent and allpowerful, take upon themselves powers that are not theirs and invade tax fields which belong to the other level of government.
IMr. Allard.]
That is why we, various members from
both sides of the house, have been asking, ever since the session began three months ago-I see some of them at their desks, others in the lobbies-in all good faith and fully aware of the implications, because of the problems which have developed in our country and of the new problems which have cropped up and did not exist in 1867, for the establishment of a joint parliamentary committee to enable us, legislators of the Canadian parliament, since we are just as intelligent as the Fathers of Confederation who, in 1867, settled the problems of their time, to solve them now together, within the framework established to that effect, rather than in the unilateral manner being followed by the present central government.
We are asking for a parliamentary committee on the constitution in order that senators and members of this house may sit here and define fairly, according to changing times and problems, a constitution within a true federalism, taking into account the disagreements and differences which exist in 1966 but which did not in 1867. That is what we are asking and what is the government doing? Nothing, it is asleep. I am looking at several members and telling them: At the next federal election, go back before the people and explain why you are preventing those who came here, in all sincerity and honesty, to settle the problems of 1966, why you prevent the members of either side from settling those problems. You are allowing such tensions and pressures to continue. Well, you will have to bear that responsibility, not only in your very heart, but also in the face of the whole country.
We are precisely requesting some reforms. Fiscal reforms are a must. Constitutional reforms are a must. It is necessary to examine problems of education, health, industrial problems within a new concept, a concept of 1966 or 1967. I cannot understand, although some members on this side of the house may call this a poor performance, how those who have come here, not to go to sleep, not to deceive the people, but to settle the problems of the country, are being refused this opportunity to establish a committee once and for all, because we Canadians, from Halifax to Vancouver, from Calgary, Fredericton, Toronto, North Bay, from everywhere, from coast to coast, need to live as brothers and with trust. But we are denied this opportunity, because initiatives which cause tensions, misunderstandings and defiance
June 21, 1966
between Canadians are allowed to become established. Mr. Speaker, that is the reason why I wanted to raise again this particular matter tonight.
I have high hopes that the present government will give serious thought to the situation before bringing forward other similar legislation. It is not only tonight's bill; recently it was the field of culture, and yesterday, that of federal loans to students, an exclusively provincial jurisdiction. [DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
The province of Quebec is not a separatist province; the province does not want separation from the rest of Canada. On the contrary, it is an hospitable province, it is a good-natured province. They do not want always to be pushed around as is done through this legislation which conflicts with the aspirations and the sacred agreements which were passed in 1867.

Health Resources Fund and it is up to them to ask for the necessary reforms. The federal government has only to give credit to these provinces so that they may develop normally without periodically going into debt.
Technology in all fields must be helped. There is no lack of young people ready to become technicians and doctors. Many would like to become doctors. Medicine is a vocation. Many young people cannot become doctors because they do not have the means.
A student must get $25,000 to $30,000 in debt to become a doctor and then incur further debts to the tune of $50,000 to buy a property, a car, everything he needs to set up practice. On top of this the people are burdened with income tax and other federal and provincial taxes. People are then unable to develop their potential. That is why many are unable to reach their goal. There is no lack of human material, but what is lacking is financial means.
And that is because the financial institution is not fulfilling its role, achieving its object. It falls directly to the Minister of Finance to reform that institution. It is the sole responsibility of that Minister and all the other ministers of the present government.
All we have to do here in Parliament is give the provinces the necessary financial institutions and means and they will take care of fiscality and education. In all fields of endeavour, provinces know what they want, know where to go. They know where to get their technicians, how to build hospitals. There is no need for the federal government to butt in everywhere. It does not have to control everything, to socialize everything. We do not want socialism; we want free enterprise; we want our citizens to be free to organize their way of life as they wish, as they see fit, according to their own aspirations. *
That is what we need in Canada, Mr. Speaker. If we cannot achieve this, and give the provinces what they need, their fiscal powers, their rights in every field of provincial jurisdiction, if we cannot do this, then we are heading toward anarchy. The provinces will not tolerate indefinitely that the federal government monopolize all powers of taxation and all powers over institutions. The provinces want to manage their own affairs, the citizens in every province want to use their own initiative, for they are capable of developing their provinces themselves.
That is why I fully support the hon. member for Sherbrooke. He is well qualified to

I ask each minister to take his responsibilities; I also ask the Minister of Finance to take his responsibilities in the financial field and to organize a financial regime which

June 21, 1966

Mr. Speaker, on June 8 I directed the following question to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources who is now, I believe, responsible for Indian affairs. The question appears at page 6139 of Hansard for that date:
Did the minister receive a petition from the Alberta Indian Teachers Association setting out certain grievances with regard to Indian schools, mentioning particularly the lack of proper medical attention and sanitation facilities? Is he aware that eight teachers have resigned because of the situation, and has he any comment to make?
Since that time there has been some discussion of Indian affairs during our consideration of the estimates. As a result of this question I asked the minister to investigate the educational, medical and other services that exist on Indian reservations, particularly in Alberta and more particularly at Morley and Gleichen in respect of the two tribes, the Stony and Blackfoot Indians. As a result of my letter to the minister I received a four page reply which in fact appeared to deny many of the facts contained in the article carried in the Calgary Herald and later in the Calgary Albertan.
I may say at the outset that any remarks I make should not be taken as criticism of the present minister, in view of the fact that he has only recently taken over this portfolio. I hope my remarks will be of some assistance to him in his thinking with reference to this matter.
My question was asked as a direct result of an article which appeared in the June 8 edition of the Calgary Herald. I do not lay
June 21. 1966
6740	COMMONS
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion any blame on the present minister tor the grievances that now exist because he has just, as I said, taken over this portfolio following reorganization. Unfortunately the ministers have changed so often as far as Indian affairs are concerned that they have failed to become knowledgeable of Indian affairs.
The letter written by the minister I am sure was of the same type that would have been written by former ministers-Mr. Nicholson, Mr. Favreau and, indeed, probably the ministers of the former government -because the department has been laying down a certain policy for so long that the Indians themselves are never asked what they consider to be the remedy for their problems in respect of education, medical services and, indeed, making a living. I once referred to this as the cod liver oil treatment. It is much like grandmother saying to a grandchild: Open your mouth, this is what you need; it is good for you.
I am sure the present minister will achieve nothing to improve the lot of Indians by continuing the policies of his predecessors, and I am sure he will not benefit by listening to the officials of his department. He could achieve more by visiting these reservations and talking to the Indians themselves.
I should like to quote from a letter written by Dr. B. A. Waldron. I know my time is limited but I should like to confirm that what he has stated in his letter of June 1, 1966 is factual on the basis of my experience during more than 25 visits to the reservations at Gleichen and Morley during the last 10 years.
I might add that before I became elected as a member of parliament I was made an honorary chief of both the Stony and Blackfoot tribes. This man has been providing medical attention to these Indians for a number of years and he states in his letter, in part:
My experience with treating these Indians has made me aware that their present medical and social welfare is at a standard far below that avail-ble to the residents of Canmore and Exshaw. I believe that the life expectancy for a Canadian Indian is half that for a Canadian European and I have knowledge of at least six deaths among Indians at Morley during the past 18 months which almost certainly would not have occurred had the medical facilities been the same as in Canmore.
I will send a copy of this letter to the minister because I do not have time to quote it all, but it points out the seriousness of the situation. For example he says that a building was constructed in Morley in 1930 when the population in the reserve was far less numerous than it is now. Although it is called a
[Mr. Woolliams.l

hospital it has not functioned as one for some years. The minister will say that those Indians are of course allowed to go into Calgary, but anybody who knows anything about the standard of living at Morley or Gleichen would know that the Indians cannot afford the gasoline for a car to take their sick people to the city of Calgary. These facts have existed for a long time, long before the present minister took over.
I am convinced the minister should be getting advice, not from his officials but from men who understand physcology, skilled anthropologists and sociologists such as Dr. Vernon Seri and Dr. Arthur Davis of the sociological department of the University of Calgary. As long as he takes advice from the same crowd of people from whom he has been getting it in the past, these Indians will continue to live in the state of poverty in which they have been for years. I do not mean this in any disrespectful way by any means but I hope the minister will ameliorate the situation and in that way make a name for himself.
I have spoken on this subject many a time. Too often we have been prone to criticize our neighbours to the south in reference to their treatment and understanding of the American negro. However, our treatment of the Canadian Indian is far more lacking in understanding. We have almost confined him to a form of concentration camp where, in some cases, he gets treaty money of $5 a year and $15 twice a year as interest on band funds. At the same time we keep eroding away the area known as the reserve. What other income has he but family allowance on which to live?
Eight teachers have resigned from the schools on the two reservations which I mentioned. I appreciate the time which the minister took to write me a letter setting out these details but the fact is that these teachers have resigned to go to other positions to which they would not be going if they were getting a fair deal on the reservation. I may say I had a conversation with one of them in reference to a letter he has written to the department, in which he said that their griev-ences were correctly set out in the newpapers but they could not afford to have their names bandied about when working as provincial employees.
