speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on June 9 last, I put the following question to the right hon. Prime Minister:
As the new or next Quebec government advocates in its program, a new alliance with the rest of the
June 21, 1366
6742	COMMONS DEBATES
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
country and the drawing up of a new Canadian constitution, does the government propose to set up shortly a joint parliamentary committee on the Canadian constitution?
The government knows that in 1963, a member of the Union Nationale, then in the opposition, moved a resolution for the establishment of a parliamentary committee on the Canadian constitution, a resolution, Mr. Speaker, which was unanimously approved at that time.
In 1964 and in 1965, that parliamentary committee in Quebec sat, heard evidence from several individuals, representatives of national associations or others, and studied five political options, namely: first, the status quo; the system which has been in operation since 1867, which I will call quasi federalism. With regard to the discrepancies in the text, there are also centralizing experiences in the confederation life over the last hundred years.
As a second option, various people commented on co-operative federalism which is, in a way, the continuation of the same system where the central government interferes in all kinds of fields coming under provincial jurisdiction and then asks the approval of the provinces-what Hon. Ren6 Levesque, with ministerial responsibilities, used to call the painless abortion of the French Canadian nation.
Consideration was also given, as a political option, to the associated state status, an independent status which in fact does not seem possible in the present circumstances.
And finally, as a last political option, which was strongly commented upon, the drafting of a new Canadian constitution setting up in the country a positive and bicultural federalism with a special status for the province of Quebec in some fields.
Mr. Speaker, that last option was in the political platform of the new Quebec government which is getting ready very soon, at ministerial meetings and at federal-provincial conferences, to request the drafting of a new Canadian constitution for such purposes.
It would be necessary, therefore, that parliament in Ottawa, the legislators in the Upper House and the other place, be in a position to state clearly, in good faith, their thoughts in a modern spirit, that of 1966, in order to engage in a dialogue on those fundamental problems.
We should not be afraid in 1966 to have the courage, the initiative and the good faith to approach all those Canadian problems, fiscal, 
constitutional, political and industrial, in order to set up the reforms necessary to a final get-together between Quebec and the other English provinces and the other ethnic groups in the country.
This is why, since the beginning of the session, many members have asked-and I am earnestly bringing up the subject again this evening-the present government to set up a joint parliamentary committee, in order that we may define more accurately together our opinions on those important matters and the proceedings of that parliamentary committee would be followed by a national constitutional conference.
I hope that the Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister will be in a position this evening to give us a favourable answer.

maintopic: CANADIAN CONSTITUTION-REQUEST ESTABLISHMENT OF JOINT PARLIAMENTARY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I fail to understand the fascination exerted on the minds of the members of the opposition and of an independent member by this notion of a joint parliamentary committee to discuss constitutional problems.
The hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Allard) mainly spoke of the problems in connection with the interests of the Quebec government. I can hardly see why the Quebec government would come here to seek within a committee we would establish the enlightenment it needs over there to form its own opinion on the constitution. True, there was created three years ago, a committee of the legislature on constitutional problems and this is explained by the fact that there were not two Quebec politicians who agreed on constitutional matters. And each referred to a particular formula, such as independence, associate states, special status and all sorts of confederations of ten independent states. They needed a parliamentary committee probably to help themselves see their way through.
As for us, we think that the role of a party government, which claims to have power at the national level, is to have a constitutional philosophy and to govern accordingly.
A committee such as proposed by the hon. member for Sherbrooke seems absolutely useless to me in this direction. Either the opposition and the independents have no constitutional philosophy, and thus that committee can only serve to give them one, and therefore that committee is of no use whatsoever; or they have a constitutional philosophy and it is in agreement with that of the government, and
June 21, 1966

then that committee serves no purpose either: or finally they have a constitutional philosophy which is at variance with that of the government, and that committee can only serve as a forum to place constitutional problems at the level of political quibbling and partisan discords.
This can in no way, in my opinion, further the constitutional debate, and I think that those ideas originate from persons who put into their minds that Canada needed to amend its constitution throughout. I suggest that this idea essentially belongs to a rising bourgeoisie which wants to change the rules of the game without taking basic needs into account.
We have a constitution, it undoubtedly needs to be applied in certain sectors-and particularly in section 133-with more vigour, and also there surely is an area where there is room for improvement, but it is the responsibility of a party, a government to have that idea. And this sort of committee as proposed to us can only be, in my opinion, a place of discord or mutual sterilization.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last week I raised the matter of the inconvenience and nuisance caused by Canadian National shunting operations in Hamilton, and I would like to elaborate on this serious problem.
About a year ago, the Canadian National moved its shunting operations eastward from the Stuart Street yards to the Parkdale yards. Unfortunately the latter is immediately adjacent to some 200 homes, and the shift has caused great distress to the inhabitants of that neighbourhood. The diesel engines in the yard create television interference over a large area. After an evening of distorted viewing, the residents are then subjected to the noises of shunting from midnight on.
I have had letters written at three or four in the morning from constituents unable to sleep because of the noise. Some have described the situation as living in a constant thunderstorm. Added to this is the soot and ash produced as freight car sweepings are burned in the Parkdale yard. This ruins house exteriors and laundry, and makes outdoor recreation impossible. It makes it necessary to keep windows closed in hot summer weather. Property values in the neighborhood
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion have fallen drastically in the past year, and the residents are fed up.
Shortly after shunting began in the Park-dale yards, a citizens committee requested that the shunting be moved a few blocks east, to a relatively unpopulated area. This was done, but after a short time operations were resumed in the Parkdale shunting yards, as before.
During last fall, this committee met with municipal, provincial and federal authorities, in the presence of some Canadian National representatives. I was present at this meeting and I was delegated to approach the Minister of Transport on behalf of these groups. I asked that the shunting be moved again to the east, a very simple matter to relieve the current nuisance.
The minister never did answer my letter which I wrote on October 26, but with customary alacrity, the department officials replied in January of 1966 with a report which indicated that consideration was being given to a number of plans to improve the situation. But there still has been no change.
Again in February of 1966 I received a letter from the Canadian National, or from representatives of the Canadian National which states in part:
The transfer of operations to some other point than Parkdale would involve extensive study in line with industrial planning in order to forecast a more favourable location for further expansion of railway facilities.
Thus, the whole situation looked rather hopeless. As I say, I have received many letters appealing that something be done. The residents of this area have lived with this grave inconvenience for over a year now. A solution to the problem is readily available a few blocks east of the shunting yards. I trust that the Department of Transport will be able to do something for the residents of this area in the very near future.
